2453Flower ornaments and other things of many kinds,
fragrant sandal and the rest — there is no counting them.

2454Hundreds of thousands of chamara whisks steal the heart with their beauty;
mridangas and many other instruments she sets out in rows.

2455She commands the parrots, cuckoos and other birds:
"Sing the endless deeds of Krishna and Radhika."

2456She tells the peacocks to dance,
and bids the bees to hum.

2457At that very moment an attendant of Vrinda
speaks very softly to Sri Vrinda-devi:

2458"Worried that the Two were late in coming, you
ordered me [to go], and I went there.

2459On Paurnamasi's advice Krishna, joyful,
was in the flower garden, watching the road for Rai.

2460Sri Radhika, coming from home with the sakhis,
met Krishna in this flower garden.

2461At the meeting of the Two Paurnamasi rejoiced
and told the Two of what you are doing."

2462Even as she was saying this, the Two arrived;
how charmingly [Their] lotus feet stepped!

2463The Two, placing Their lovely arms on each other's shoulders,
absorbed in rasa, stand gazing at each other.

2464In the telling, there is no limit to that beauty;
in the gazing, the eyes forget to blink.

2465The radiance of the beauty of the Two lights up the three worlds,
putting to shame the mass of rain clouds and the lightning.

2466Surrounded by the sakhis headed by Lalita, [They] are exceedingly beautiful;
the radiance of the bodies of all [the sakhis] sparkles.

2467With wondrous grace they walk into the depths of the kunja;
softly, softly, ceaselessly the anklets ring.

2468Rai and Kanu, entering the kunja with the sakhis,
joyfully behold the splendor Vrinda has arranged.

2469Smiling, the Two sit on that wonderful throne;
all around, the sakhis in their bliss forget themselves.

2470Hundreds of thousands of maidservants fan [Them] with chamara whisks;
the parrots, cuckoos and other [birds] sing the qualities of the Two.

2471The bees hum like the sweetest music;
all around the peacocks and peahens dance.

2472At Vrinda's bidding all displayed their own skills;
in this way Vrinda made her heart's desire known.

2473Most clever Krishna, rasa embodied,
smiling, what He said to Vrinda with the corner of His eye!

2474As Vrinda offered sandal and the rest, and the flower ornaments,
the merriment that grew — who can describe it?

2475Lalita, opening that casket of tambula,
was delighted, placing tambula in Rai's hand.

2476Sri Radhika, joyfully taking a roll of tambula,
with a graceful gesture placed [it] in Krishna's moon-like mouth.

2477Softly, softly Krishna smiles, His heart impatient;
chewing the tambula, He displays many playful moods.

2478Intending to enjoy the Sri rasa pastimes,
He gazes at Rai's face with a wondrous grace.

2479Krishna is the embodiment of bliss, the treasury of rasa;
His grace surpasses millions upon millions of Kandarpas.

2480The peacock feather on His head shines without end;
the flute is placed at His lips — how sweet [His] attire!

2481To fulfil Vrinda's desire,
Krishna sports here together with Sri Radhika.

2482His beloveds are countless; among them the best is Radha,
who fulfils all of Sri Krishna's longings.

2483Who can describe what Radhika's attire is like?
For the attire of Lalita and the others no comparison can be found.

2484Radhika's companions are beyond counting;
the hosts of sakhis headed by Lalita have no end.

2485Surrounded by hundreds of thousands of young beauties,
Krishna sports with His arm upon Rai's shoulder.

2486In the Sri rasa pastimes beauty filled the world;
everyone became immersed in sangita.617

2487What can be said? Wondrous are the ways of sangita:
captivating every heart, it is spread everywhere.

2488O Srinivasa! Long ago Brahma, from the Vedas,
revealed the Sangita-veda — [this] is known to the world.

2489Thus [it is said]:
Long ago the Lotus-born, drawing out the essence of the four Vedas,
fashioned this fifth Veda, called sangita.

2490Sama, Rig, Atharva and the rest — the four Vedas;
from them are born song, recitation, rasa and acting.

2491Thus [it is said]:
From the Riks arose recitation, from the Samans song was born,
from the Yajuses acting was born, and the rasas are held to come from the Atharva.

2492Brahma, Shiva and others are the propagators of this sangita;
it, the sweetest of all, pervades all the worlds.

2493Thus [it is said]:
Brahma, Isha, Nandi, Bharata, Durga, Narada, Kohala,
Dashasya, Vayu, Rambha and others are the propagators of sangita.618

2494Sangita in its essence is three: song, instrumental music and dance;
some call two — song and instrumental music — sangita.

2495The power of song, dance and instrumental music is immense:
it captivates the hearts of all — gods, humans and others.

2496Thus [it is said] in the Sangita-parijata:619
Song, instrumental music and dance — this triad is called sangita;
because song is the chief among them, it is named sangita.

2497In the Sangita-shiromani:
Song, instrumental music and dance — this triad is called sangita;
some [say] that sangita is only song and instrumental music together.
It is celebrated as captivating the minds of animals, humans, gods and others.620

2498Sangita is of two kinds — by the distinction of marga and deshi.
In heaven is [the sangita] based on marga; its teacher is Brahma.

2499Deshi, [varying] by the various lands, abides on earth.
Thus these two — marga and deshi — are well known in the shastras.

2500Thus [it is said] in the Sangita-sara:
By the distinction of marga and deshi, sangita is twofold:
that based on marga is in heaven; that based on deshi delights the earth.

2501In the Sangita-parijata:
By the distinction of marga and deshi, sangita is said to be twofold.
The sangita called marga the Creator himself told to Bharata.

2502Bharata, having learned from Brahma the sangita called marga,
performed it before Shambhu together with the apsaras and gandharvas.

2503And sangita [that varies] by the difference of lands they call deshi.

2504The cause of the origin of song and the rest is nada;
nada is Hari Himself; who can know the truth of nada?

2505Thus [it is said]:
Without nada there is no song, without nada there is no svara,
without nada there is no raga — therefore the world consists of nada.621

2506In the Sangita-damodara:
Without nada there is no knowledge, without nada there is no Shiva.
The supreme light has the form of nada; Hari Himself has the form of nada.

2507Anjaneya [says]:622
Sarasvati does not know the farther shore of the ocean of nada:
even today, fearing to drown, she carries a gourd upon her breast.

2508Nada arises from fire and air;
from ether and the other [elements], and from air too, that nada is born.

2509The place where nada is born is below the navel;
rising above the navel, it is finally manifested in the mouth.

2510The ways [of describing] how nada arises are many;
some define the arising of nada briefly.

2511Thus [it is said] in the Sangita-sara:
The syllable "na" is the life-breath (prana-vayu), the syllable "da" is fire;
because it is born from these two, therefore it is called nada.623

2512That is, nada is born from these two — prana and fire.

2513In the Sangita-muktavali:
That which, born of ether, fire and air and rising above the navel,
comes to manifestation in the mouth is called nada.

2514Nada is threefold: it occurs in the living, it occurs also in the non-living,
and it is also possible from the union of the living and the non-living — these are the three.

2515[The nada] of the living is born of the body; that which is without a living body is determined as the non-living; the flute and the like are known as [sources of nada] from the living and the non-living.

2516The sound arises through air touching the mouth and nose;
therefore [it] is said to be born of the living and the non-living.

2517Thus [it is said]:
And it is born of the living, born of the non-living, and arises from both:
the first is born of the body, the second arises from the vina,
and the third arises from the flute and the like — thus it is held to be threefold.

2518In practice nada is threefold — mandra, madhya and tara:
by their places — in the heart, in the throat, in the head — in order; so it is known.624

2519Madhya is twice as high as mandra,
tara is twice as high as madhya — these are the three.

2520Thus [it is said]:
In practice the wise call this nada threefold:
mandra abides in the heart, madhya in the throat, and tara in the head;
each following one, it is said, is twice the preceding in measure.

2521Such is the origin of nada and the way of knowing nada.
In the rasa dance the gopis pour forth song.

2522The power of sangita — [revealed] in the song that pours from the gopis' mouths for Krishna's delight — is declared in all the shastras.

2523Thus [it is said]:
Even those versed in shruti, smriti and other literature and in the various shastras,
if they do not know sangita, are considered two-footed beasts.

2524Knowledge, sacrifices, hymns and all the rest give the fruits of the trivarga;
the knowledge of sangita alone bestows the fruits of the chaturvarga.625

2525It is said in particular in the Sangita-damodara:
He in whose heart there is no joy from charming sangita
is an ox among men in [this] world: he has been cheated by the Creator himself.

2526By song deer and even birds are taken captive;
snakes come helplessly, and children do not cry.

2527Increasing supreme bliss, granting the desired fruit, subduing,
stealing the hearts of all people, the seed of liberation — supreme is song.

2528O Srinivasa! Krishna, the abode of rasa,
the crest-jewel of those who know song, sports in the rasa dance.

2529Supreme, wondrous beauty is in the Sri rasa-mandala;
with rapture they display song to one another.

2530The characteristics of song are of many kinds;
widely known is song with dhatu and matu.626

2531These dhatu and matu awaken attraction;
dhatu is the component of song, matu is raga and the rest.

2532In the Sangita-sara:
Song is delightful, being joined with dhatu and matu.

2533The component of song is dhatu; raga and the rest is called matu.

2534Dhatu is "nadatmaka" — on this there is much deliberation.
"Nadatmaka" means that whose "atma," [that is,] own nature, is nada.

2535In the Narada-samhita:
Song is said to be [that which is] joined with dhatu and matu;
of these, that which is sung and consists of nada is called dhatu.

2536Here the word "nada" [covers] the shrutis and svaras born of nada,
the murchhanas, the so-called talas, the gramas — a great many kinds.627

2537From nada many shrutis are born;
from the shrutis are born the svaras — shadja and the rest.

2538From the svaras murchhanas are born; from the murchhanas
the so-called talas, arising from the gramas; [this] is known to the world.628

2539Thus [it is said]:
From nada the shrutis were born, from them the svaras, shadja and the rest,
from them arise the murchhanas, from them the so-called talas, born of the gramas.

2540O Srinivasa! In keeping with this subject,
the order of which I shall speak I set forth in few words.

2541Nada, shruti, svara, grama, murchhana — [so] it is established;
tala, varna, graha-svara and amsha-svara,

2542nyasa-svara, jati — all these in this order
I shall set forth briefly; others expound them in detail.

2543Thus [it is said]:
Nada, shruti, svara, grama, murchhana, tala, varna,
the svaras called graha, amsha and nyasa, and jati — here in this order.629

2544I have told of nada; now learn of shruti and the rest,
which Krishna with His beloveds reveals in song in the rasa dance.

2545O Srinivasa! In this Sri rasa-mandala —
what shall I say! — all these took embodied form.

2546How the shrutis become manifest from nada —
in revealing this, Krishna's playful delight is boundless.

2547That nada, struck by air, [becomes] twenty-two shrutis;
twenty-two nadis, [running] crosswise and upward, are situated in the heart.630

2548As many nadis, so many shrutis — this is known everywhere;
ascending in order, higher and higher, they are discerned on the vina and [other instruments].

2549In a throat spoiled by phlegm and the like the shrutis are not manifest.
Thus everyone explains [this] in many ways.

2550Thus [it is said] on the shrutis:
That nada, struck by air, becomes twenty-two shrutis;
twenty-two nadis, [running] crosswise and upward, are situated in the heart.

2551As many as they are, so many shrutis are declared;
ascending in order, higher and higher, they are discerned only on the vina and [other instruments],
since in a throat spoiled by phlegm and the like they do not become manifest.

2552The twenty-two shrutis among the seven svaras beginning with shadja —
the order of their division the best of the learned state thus:

2553madhyama, panchama and shadja have four shrutis [each],
the svara rishabha and the svara dhaivata have three shrutis [each],631

2554gandhara and nishada have two — these are the twenty-two.
From the shrutis the svaras are born — this is very well known.

2555Thus [it is said]:
Four shrutis are held to belong to panchama, shadja and madhyama,
three to rishabha and dhaivata, two to gandhara and nishada.

2556The names of the shrutis differ in different regions;
I shall name those accepted by many, from which shadja and the rest are born.

2557Nandi, Vishala, Sumukhi and Vichitra — these four;
from them is born the svara shadja, captivating all hearts.

2558Chitra, Ghana and Kandalika — these three in rishabha;
in gandhara, Saragha and Mala — two shruti names.632

2559In the svara madhyama, Magadhi, Shiva, Matangika
and Maitreyi: these four excel in every respect.

2560Bala, Kala, Kalarava and Sharngaravi by name —
in panchama these four incomparable shrutis.

2561Mata, Rasa and Amrita — these three in dhaivata;
in nishada, Vijaya and Madhukari — two shrutis.633

2562Thus [it is said]:
Nandi, Vishala, Sumukhi and Vichitra are known as shadjas
("shadjas," that is, those that generate shadja);
Chitra, Ghana and Kandalika — three — are named in rishabha.

2563In gandhara, Saragha and Mala; in madhyama, Magadhi, Shiva,
Matangika and Maitreyi — four are declared.

2564Bala, Kala, Kalarava and also Sharngaravi in panchama;
Yata, Rasa and Amrita — three — in the one named dhaivata.

2565And two in the one named nishada: Vijaya and also Madhukari.
Thus the twenty-two shrutis of the svaras are stated.
(In the words "shrutis of the svaras" the genitive expresses the relation of the generated and the generator, as in "the father of the sons"; the meaning is "generating the svaras.")

2566Other names of the shrutis are Siddhi, Prabhavati and the rest;
in this there are many more varieties as well.

2567Thus [it is said] in Kohala:
Siddhi, Prabhavati, Kanta and Subhadra, the charming ones,
issued from the mouth of Prajapati, produce the svara shadja.
And so on.

2568How the svaras [lie] in the places of the shrutis the universe does not know;
the knowers of sangita merely describe [their] characteristics.634

2569Thus [it is said]:
Even Brahma cannot truly name the svaras in the places of the shrutis:
the path of fish moving in the waters is not to be traced.

2570O Srinivasa! Who knows the true nature of the shrutis?
Only in the rasa dance did it become manifest — in charming song.

2571As Krishnachandra makes the shrutis known,
so Sri Radhika wondrously manifests [them].

2572The joy of Lalita and the other sakhis is boundless;
the gods, filled with wonder, shower flowers.

2573The shrutis praise each its own good fortune;
the shrutis together with the svaras attract every heart.

2574Now, the svaras:
That which in the place of a shruti delights the heart is svara;
or: all the svaras captivate the listener.

2575Thus [it is said]:
Svara is that which, manifesting in the place of a shruti, delights the heart;
by this the word "svara" is said to be yoga-rudha.
Or else: because they delight the listener's mind, therefore [they] are svaras.635

2576The names of the seven svaras are shadja, rishabha, gandhara,
madhyama, panchama, dhaivata and also nishada.

2577Sa, ri, ga, ma, pa, dha, ni are their other names;
the seven svaras have three states — mandra, madhya and tara.

2578The places of these three, in order, are the heart, the throat and the head;
from mandra the song is [each time] twice, twice as high.

2579Thus [it is said]:
Shadja and rishabha, gandhara, madhyama and also panchama,
dhaivata and nishada — here seven svaras are named.

2580Sa, ri, ga, ma, pa, dha, ni — these are their other names.
They are threefold, abiding in the states of mandra, madhya and tara.

2581For they have three places: mandra arises in the heart,
madhya in the throat, tara in the head; each following one is twice [as high].

2582How the seven svaras beginning with shadja arise,
the knowers of sangita have proclaimed with great delight.

2583Among them, the svara shadja:
Chest, nose, throat, palate, tongue and teeth —
in these six places the svara shadja is born.

2584Thus [it is said]:
Because it is born from six, touching the nose, throat, chest, palate,
tongue and teeth, therefore it is known as shadja.636

2585But Damodara says otherwise:
Air, intensified in the navel, in the nadi and in the heart,
in the two sides and in the head — from [these] six shadja is born.637

2586Thus in the shastras it is well established how the svara shadja arises;
the origin of rishabha and the other svaras is simply set forth.

2587Now, the svara rishabha:
When air, rising from the root of the navel, produces a sound
and issues forth easily, like [the bellow] of a bull, [it] is known as rishabha.638

2588Now, the svara gandhara:
Air, rising from the navel and setting [sound] in motion in the throat and in the ear,
issues forth with sound — therefore [the svara] is called gandhara.639

2589Now, the svara madhyama:
Madhyama is born from the middle place of the body
and from the root of the navel; by nature it is deep, [yet] somewhat high.

2590Now, the svara panchama:
Prana, apana, samana, and likewise udana and vyana —
from their union the svara panchama is born.640

2591He states the fixed places of these:
prana is in the heart, apana in the anus, samana is in the middle of the navel,
udana abides in the region of the throat, vyana pervades the whole body.

2592Now, the svara dhaivata:
That which, going to the lower part of the navel and reaching the bladder, rises upward again
and goes as if running to the region of the throat — that is dhaivata.

2593Now, the svara nishada:
Since here these six svaras, shadja and the rest, all charming, sit down,
therefore it is called nishada in the world.641

2594Know the forms of the seven svaras according to the doctrine of similar sounds:
the peacock utters the svara shadja — [this] is known to the world.

2595The chataka — rishabha, the goat — gandhara,
the krauncha — the one called madhyama, the cuckoo — panchama: so it is held.642

2596The frog — dhaivata; the elephant utters the svara nishada.
Such are the forms of the svaras; some state another view.

2597Thus [it is said]:
The peacock utters shadja, the chataka speaks rishabha,
the goat proclaims gandhara, the krauncha voices madhyama,

2598the cuckoo sings panchama, the frog voices dhaivata,
the elephant utters nishada — this is accepted by Brahma and others.

2599But Damodara [says]:
The peacock, the bull, the goat, the krauncha, the cuckoo, the horse
and the elephant, in order, utter these svaras, so hard to attain.

2600Further, these seven svaras have four designations:
vadi, samvadi, vivadi and anuvadi.643

2601Among the seven svaras, vadi is the name of the svara
which, through frequent use, determines the raga and the rest.

2602[The svara] with shrutis equal to panchama's is samvadi;
sometimes the svara madhyama is not samvadi.

2603Gandhara, nishada, and also rishabha, dhaivata —
these four are vivadi, enemies: [so] it is firmly accepted in the shastras.

2604In another view, the svaras rishabha and dhaivata, and also
gandhara and nishada, are vivadi: so it is held.

2605The svara that remains of all these svaras
the best of the learned call the anuvadi svara.

2606Thus [it is said]:
Further, the svaras, called vadi, samvadi, vivadi and anuvadi,
are declared to be of four kinds; of these, vadi is said to be the one

2607which, abundant in use, indicates the determination of the raga and the rest;
[the svara] with shrutis equal to panchama's is samvadi; sometimes it is not [so].

2608Ga and ni are vivadi to ri and dha, or else those two to these two;
the remaining one is anuvadi — such is Dattila's view.644

2609The vadi svara is the king, the samvadi is determined to be the minister;
the vivadi svara is the enemy: this is held everywhere.

2610The anuvadi is the retinue of the king and the minister;
all these natures are beyond the grasp of others.

2611Thus [it is said]:
The vadi is the king, the samvadi the minister, and the vivadi the enemy;
the anuvadi is declared to be the servant of the king and the minister.

2612O Srinivasa! All these charming svaras
Krishna, the crown of rasikas, reveals in song.

2613Before Krishna Lalita sings, taking up the vina,
skilled in manifesting the forms of the svaras and the rest.

2614Hearing [this], the gandharvas are ashamed at heart:
who can understand the longing that they feel?

2615The svaras deem themselves blessed;
the wondrous course of the svaras is manifested in the gramas.

2616Now, the gramas:
The combining of the subtle states of the svaras is called grama;
shadja, madhyama and gandhara are the names of the three gramas.

2617The two — shadja and madhyama — are known on earth;
in the world of the gods gandhara is esteemed — by every view.

2618Among the three gramas the shadja-grama is the best;
the grama is the basis of the murchhanas: so the shastras determine.

2619Thus [it is said]:
Grama is the subtlest state of the svaras,
[their] combination, the assemblage of places; it is threefold:
shadja and likewise madhyama are on earth,
while the one named gandhara is indeed in the world of the gods.

2620And further:
A group of well-arranged svaras is considered a grama.

2621In the Sangita-parijata:
Further, the gramas are declared to be three, having the form of a collection of svaras;
they are endowed with the names shadja, madhyama and gandhara;
they are the basis of the murchhanas; of the three, the shadja-grama is the best.

2622In the three gramas the seven svaras are manifested as murchhanas;
in the shadja-grama it is established: sa-ri-ga-ma-pa-dha-ni.

2623Ma-pa-dha-ni-sa-ri-ga is in the madhyama-grama;
ga-ma-pa-dha-ni-sa-ri in gandhara — this is certain.

2624In the Parijata:645
Sa-ri-ga-ma-pa-dha-ni, and ma-pa-dha-ni-sa-ri-ga,
and ga-ma-pa-dha-ni-sa-ri are the murchhanas of the three gramas.

2625Others too [say]:
Sa-ri-ga-ma-pa-dha-ni — these are the murchhanas of the shadja-grama;
ma-pa-dha-ni-sa-ri-ga — the murchhanas of the madhyama-grama;
ga-ma-pa-dha-ni-sa-ri — the murchhanas of the gandhara-grama.

2626Thus in each grama the seven svaras are amply unfolded;
by the order of all the distinctions there are twenty-one kinds.

2627All this is known; [so] Bharata and others define it:
jati, shruti, svara and the rest attain [the nature of] grama.

2628Kohala too [says]:
Through the jatis and shrutis the svaras attain the nature of grama.

2629O Srinivasa! In this sweet Vrindavana,
in supreme bliss, in the rasa dance, Krishna together with His beloved

2630reveals the three gramas in various ways,
at which wonder arises in Shiva, Brahma and the others.

2631Radhika, praising the Lord of her life again and again,
conducts the grama so that Krishna is struck with wonder.

2632Losing His composure, Krishna embraces Rai;
the jubilation of the sakhis headed by Lalita is boundless.

2633What playful delight is in that song — what power have I to tell it?
In the three gramas the murchhanas appear in various ways.

2634Now the murchhanas.
The murchhana is born of the grama, Bharata says.
The svara, unfolding in the grama, becomes raga.

2635Thus [it is said]:
Where the svara, being unfolded, attains the nature of raga,
that the [followers of] Bharata call murchhana, born of the grama.646

2636And further:
Where the svara, merely by being unfolded, has attained the nature of raga —
that the sage calls murchhana.
Born of the grama, joined with the seven svaras,
in the three sthanas they again [number] twenty-one.647

2637In the three gramas there are thrice seven murchhanas of the svaras;
the murchhanas are named Lalita, Madhyama, Chitra and the rest.648

2638Thus [it is said]:
Lalita, Madhyama, Chitra, Rohini and Matangaja,
Sauvira, Varnamadhya, Shadjamadhya and Panchami,

2639Matsari, Mridumadhya, Shuddhanta and Kalavati,
Tivra, Raudri, and also Brahmi, Vaishnavi, Khechari, Vara,

2640Nadavati and Vishala — renowned in the three gramas:
thus the Moon-crested One named the twenty-one murchhanas.649

2641By the knowledge of the murchhanas happiness grows at every moment;
Bharata and others tell the purpose of murchhana.

2642Thus [it is said]: Performing a murchhana at the crown of the head, even the slayer of a brahmana is freed.650

2643O Srinivasa! The murchhana is born of the grama;
what kinds there are in it — that other people do not know.

2644Together with His beloveds Krishna, in the joy of His heart,
reveals [them] in a wondrous manner in the rasa pastimes.

2645What shall I say! Krishna, the crown of great rasikas,
unfolds many talas and charming songs.

2646Now the talas.651
The murchhanas are indeed the talas, the pure ones and the others;
the talas are born of the seven svaras — so too it is defined.

2647The talas are forty-nine: [so] it is proclaimed in the shastras;
separately there are the kuta-talas, very numerous.

2648They are five thousand and thirty-three;
the names of the talas are many, their power immense.

2649Thus [it is said]:
The murchhanas themselves, based on ascent, are the pure talas.

2650But Damodara [says]:652
Those by which the applications [of the svaras], resting on the remainder of the murchhana, are unfolded —
those are the talas, forty-nine in number, born of the seven svaras.

2651From them alone arise others — the kuta-talas, each separately;
their varieties are very many — who will tell them in full?

2652The many varieties of the gramas, murchhanas and talas
are not stated, since they are of no use for the present subject and are unknowable.

2653This is said in the section on talas:
These talas are five thousand and thirty-three.

2654Having praised Shiva with the agnishtomika tala, one becomes auspicious.
Here the pure talas have names — Agnishtoma and the rest —653

2655but, owing to their unfitness for practice, I have not listed them.654

2656The good fortune of these talas is immense:
taking embodied form, they sport before Krishna.

2657Lalita and the other sakhis of Radhika, the group leaders (yutheshvaris),
each separately set the talas in motion.

2658Rai and Kanu, in supreme bliss, together with the sakhis
reveal varna and song in wondrous arrangements.655

2659Now varna is described.
The svara employed at the beginning of the act of singing is varna;
it is of four kinds, by which the singer is gladdened.

2660Sthayi varna, the arohi and avarohi varnas, and also
sanchari — the characteristics of these four are proclaimed.

2661When one and the same svara is used with pauses again and again,
it is sthayi varna — so it is acknowledged in all views.

2662The arohi and avarohi svaras [after] sthayi are according to the sense [of their names]; the varna in which these three are mixed is accepted as sanchari.656

2663Thus [it is said]:
The svara employed at the beginning of the act of singing is called varna;
it is of four kinds: sthayi, arohi, avarohi and sanchari.

2664The definition of each:
If one and the same svara is used with pauses again and again,
that is to be known as sthayi varna; the other two have names according to their sense.
The other two are the arohi svara and the avarohi svara; they "have names according to their sense," that is, their names follow their meaning: the sense is — "arohi" in the meaning "it ascends," "avarohi" — "it descends."

2665In the Sangita-parijata:
If the use is with pauses again and again on each single svara,
that is to be known as sthayi varna; the other two have names according to their sense;
the varna [arising] from their mixture is called sanchari.
"Their" — [that is,] of the sthayi, arohi and avarohi svaras.

2666Sa-ri-ga-ma-pa-dha-ni — these varnas are the seven svaras;
by particular arrangements [of them there arise] a great many alankaras.657

2667Thus [it is said]:
The varnas become alankaras through the particularities of arrangement.

2668The sthayi are twenty-six, the arohi certainly twelve,
the avarohi twelve, the sanchari twelve.

2669All together there are sixty-two kinds of alankaras;
among them are many varieties — [this] is proclaimed in the shastras.

2670Thus [it is said]:
The sthayi are twenty-six, the arohi twelve,
the sanchari twelve and the avarohi twelve.
Thus the sixty-two well-known alankaras are proclaimed.

2671The purposes of alankara are many:
the shastras name the strengthening of practice in the knowledge of the svaras and so on.

2672Thus [it is said]:
Firm practice in the knowledge of the svaras and the attainment of delight arise;
variety in the knowledge of the varnas — [such is] the purpose of alankara.

2673In the Sangita-parijata:
Without alankaras the ragas do not attain expansion.

2674On sthayi varna.
The guidance on the alankaras of sthayi varna is given thus:
the varna on which [the figure] begins comes again at the end.

2675Here I explain the alankara named Bhadra:
its arrangement is an order in which one svara at a time is dropped.

2676Thus [it is said] in the Parijata:
Where, beginning [from a svara] and going on to the next, one again utters the previous svara —
that alankara the wise Anjaneya called Bhadra.
Here the order [is formed] by dropping one svara at a time.
Example: sa-ri-sa, ri-ga-ri, ga-ma-ga, ma-pa-ma, pa-dha-pa, dha-ni-dha, ni-sa-ni, sa-ri-sa.

2677On arohi varna.
Thus I point the way in the arohi alankaras:
[the alankara] named Vistirna has long varnas on the seven svaras.

2678In the Parijata:
Where from the initial svara of the murchhana there is ascent in order
with long svaras, pausing on each, that [alankara] is called Vistirna.
Example: sā rī gā mā pā dhā nī.

2679The first two [svaras] short, the third syllable long —
[this] is the charming alankara named Prachchhadana.

2680In the Parijata:
Making the first two short and making the third long —
[this] the all-knowing Hanuman calls the excellent Sandhi-prachchhadana.658
Example: sa-ri-gā, ri-ga-mā, ga-ma-pā, ma-pa-dhā, pa-dha-nī, dha-ni-sā.

2681[The alankara] named Udvahita: the first [svara] is uttered four times,
the second twice, the third and fourth once each.

2682In the Parijata:
The first svara four times, the second twice;
uttering the third once and likewise the fourth once —
[this] is the alankara Udvahita, proclaimed by Hanuman.659
Example: sa-sa-sa-sa ri-ri ga ma, ri-ri-ri-ri ga-ga ma pa, ga-ga-ga-ga ma-ma pa dha, ma-ma-ma-ma pa-pa dha ni, pa-pa-pa-pa dha-dha ni sa.

2683On avarohi varna.
The avarohi alankaras are of the same kind;
to speak [of them] is superfluous — others too do not speak of them.

2684In the Parijata:
These [same], in descending order, are the twelve avarohi;
because of the prolixity I have not written out the descent.

2685On sanchari varna.
It moves everywhere — therefore it [is called] sanchari;
I point the way, by which the singer has joy.

2686The first two varnas are repeated three times; after that
the third varna, and after it the second syllable.

2687Thus is described the alankara named Prasada;
in knowing all this there is joy — [so] it is proclaimed in the shastras.

2688In the Parijata:
And since they move about everywhere, therefore [they are] sanchari.

2689Repeating the first pair three times and uttering the third and [then] the second,
the wise have called that alankara Prasada.
Example: sa-ri sa-ri sa-ri ga-ri, ri-ga ri-ga ri-ga ma-ga, ga-ma ga-ma ga-ma pa-ma, ma-pa ma-pa ma-pa dha-pa, pa-dha pa-dha pa-dha ni-dha, dha-ni dha-ni dha-ni sa-ni.

2690Here there is one alankara named Akshepa:
three svaras are uttered in order, beginning from the first.

2691In the Parijata:
Where three svaras [go] in order, that the wise have called Akshepaka.
Example: sa-ri-ga, ri-ga-ma, ga-ma-pa, ma-pa-dha, pa-dha-ni, dha-ni-sa.

2692The varna named Kokila is like the lion's backward glance:
sa-ri-ga, sa-ri-ga-ma — such is its manner.660

2693In the Parijata:
Sa-ri-ga and sa-ri-ga-ma — from these Kokila arises.
Example: sa-ri-ga sa-ri-ga-ma, ri-ga-ma ri-ga-ma-pa, ga-ma-pa ga-ma-pa-dha, ma-pa-dha ma-pa-dha-ni, pa-dha-ni pa-dha-ni-sa.

2694All these varna-alankaras on the svaras are sweet;
[He] utters them so that sorrow goes far away.

2695From the lovely moon-like face of Sri Krishnachandra
nectar seems to flow in the form of varna-alankaras.

2696Sri Radhika, together with the sakhis headed by Lalita,
sings the varna-alankaras with supremely wondrous delight.

2697The pride of the gandharvas and the others was shattered;
there is no comparison in the world — so sweet [it is].

2698Praising everyone, Krishna with a joyful heart
gazes with unblinking eyes at Rai's face.

2699Graha-svara, amsha-svara and nyasa-svara — these three —
Krishna, the abode of rasa, playfully reveals.

2700Now [it is told] of the graha-svara:
The svara among the seven that is placed at the beginning of a song and the like —
that the sages Bharata and others call the graha-svara.

2701Thus [it is said]:
That is called the graha-svara which is placed at the beginning of a song and the like.

2702And in the Sangita-parijata:
That which is set at the beginning of a song and the like is called the graha-svara.

2703Now [it is told] of the amsha-svara:
The amsha-svara reveals anuraga in song;
Bharata and others thus describe its great power.

2704Thus [it is said]:
That which in song reveals charm, which all [the others] follow,
which itself becomes graha in the use of nyasa and the rest,
which abounds everywhere — that amsha, the vadi, is like a king.661

2704a"The vadi is that which determines the raga and the rest," [says] the author of the Gita-prakasha. By the words "which itself becomes graha" it is meant that the amsha-svara is the cause of the graha-svara.662

2705And further:
Those that are called the life of the ragas the wise call amsha-svaras.

2706In the Sangita-parijata:
That which abounds in use is called the amsha-svara.663

2707Now [it is told] of the nyasa-svara:
The nyasa-svara brings a song and the like to completion;
he who knows this attains bliss.

2708Thus [it is said]:
The nyasa-svara is declared to be that which completes a song and the like.

2709Likewise in the Sangita-parijata:
The nyasa-svara should be known as that which concludes a song.

2710O Srinivasa! Krishna, absorbed in the rapture of rasa,
reveals the arrangement of the graha-, amsha- and nyasa-svaras.

2711So that Shiva, Brahma and others are astonished,
He spreads forth the svaras, the jatis and the rest.

2712Now [it is told] of jati:
That from which a raga is born is called jati;
it is the mother of the raga; further, the kinds of jati are three.

2713That called shuddha, that called vikrita, and from the union of these two
that called sankirna — these three the wise speak of.664

2714Thus [it is said]:
That from which the raga is born is here jati; she is also the mother of the raga.
[She is] threefold: called shuddha, vikrita, and from the union of the two, sankirnaka.

2715The seven shuddha jatis are named after the svaras, shadja and the rest;
those born of the shuddha are vikrita, say the learned.

2716Those called vikrita are eleven, the shastras determine;
the remaining, called sankirna, are born of the vikrita.

2717Shuddha and vikrita — these are eighteen kinds;
these two [kinds] the acharyas accepted.

2718The shuddha jatis bear the names Shadji, Arshabhi and so on;
the vikrita bear the names Shadja-kaishiki and so on.

2719Shadja-kaishiki is born from the union of Shadji and Gandhari;
so [arise] those called vikrita — [this] is known everywhere.

2720Thus [it is said]:
The shuddha jatis are seven; they are named after the svaras, shadja and the rest.
They themselves [become] vikrita; the remaining are born of the mixture of the vikrita.

2721Others [say]: "Thus [the jatis] are twofold." This was stated by Harinayaka:
"Taken together, the shuddha and the vikrita jatis are declared to be eighteen;
they are the mothers of the ragas."
This very view seems to be the principal one, since it was accepted by the ancient acharyas.665

2722This is stated in another treatise:
Shadji, Arshabhi, Gandhari, Madhyami and likewise Panchami,
Dhaivati and then Naishadi — these seven are the shuddha jatis.

2723There are Shadja-kaishiki, and after it Shadja-madhyama,
Gandhara-panchami, Andhri, and likewise Shadjodichyavati,666

2724Karmavari, Nandayanti, and also Gandharodichchara,
Madhyamodichchara, Rakta-gandhari and also Kaishiki.667

2725Thus eleven vikrita are declared by Bharata and others.
Now we shall state the causes [of the origin] of the vikrita formed from the shuddha.668

2726From the union of Shadji and Gandhari is born Shadja-kaishiki;
from Shadji and Madhyami is born Shadja-madhyama;
from Gandhari and Panchami is born Gandhara-panchami — and so on.

2727The kinds of connection of these eighteen with the gramas
Bharata and other authors of books have described in detail.

2728From shruti at the beginning to jati at the end — [all] I have told briefly;
know that all this is in part made manifest on the vina.

2729Thus [it is said]:
Whatever I have set forth, beginning with shruti and ending with jati,
all that the wise may know in part only on the vinas, and not otherwise.

2730The jatis, mothers of the ragas, took embodied form in the rasa dance;
they deem [this] their own good fortune — there is no end to telling.

2731O Srinivasa! The rasa pastime is above all;
who knows how to tell what the sweetness of [that] song is like?

2732The sound of the voices of Rai and Kanu, surpassing the sound of the vina,
reveals the jatis, at which the sakhis rejoice.

2733When [They] reveal the ragas, each one separately,
what delight increases — who can describe it?

2734Now [it is told] of raga:
Bharata and others give this definition of raga:
the ragas tinge [with delight] the hearts of [beings] in the three worlds.

2735Sixteen thousand ragas the shastras determine;
all of them shine on the four sides of Meru.669

2736Among all these ragas thirty-six ragas
are renowned in the world — so say all the knowers.

2737Thus [it is said]:
Those by which the hearts of those dwelling in the three worlds are tinged [with delight]
are called ragas — [so say] the sages Bharata and others.

2738In the Narada-panchama-sara-samhita:670
Krishna began sangita, enchanting [all] with the sound of the flute;
in Krishna's presence the gopis began to sing, each one [her own song];
from that sixteen thousand ragas were born.

2739And further:
Of these ragas, thirty-six ragas are renowned in the world;
and all of them, too, abide on the four sides of Meru, [say] some.

2740Of the thirty-six: six ragas and thirty raginis;
each raga has five wives — this too is well accepted.671

2741The six ragas are Bhairava and the rest; in order, for these six,
the raginis are Bhairavi and the rest, known in the shastras.

2742Thus [it is said] in the Sangita-damodara:
Bhairava, then Vasanta, the raga Malava-kaishika,
the raga Shri, the raga Megha and likewise Nata-narayana.672

2743These are the six male ragas; in order I shall name their raginis:
Bhairavi, Kaishiki, and also Bhasha, Velavali673

2744and Vangali — these raginis are here the beloveds of Bhairava.
Andolita, Deshakhya, Lola, Prathama-manjari
and Mallari — these raginis always follow Vasanta.

2745Gauri, Gunakiri, and also Varadi and Kshamavati
and Karnati — these raginis are dear to Malava-kaishika.

2746Gandhari, Deva-gandhari, Malavashri, Savari
and also Ramakiri — these raginis are dear to the raga Shri.

2747Lalita, Malasi, Gauri, Nati and likewise Devakiri —
these raginis are the raga Megha's own beloveds.

2748Taramani, Svadhabhiri, Kamodi and likewise Gurjari
and Kakubha — these raginis are dear to Nata-narayana.

2749Some say: six ragas and thirty-six raginis,
each raga has six wives — and this too is quite consistent [with the shastras].

2750Thus [it is said] in the Narada-panchama-sara-samhita:
The ragas are six, and the raginis thirty-six, of lovely form.
The raga consists of Shiva and Shakti; [it is] an ocean of the rasa of supreme prema:
by merely hearing it Vishnu melted.

2751Among them, the ragas:
Malava, Mallara, the raga Shri and Vasantaka,
then Hindola and Karnata — [thus] the six male ragas are celebrated.674

2752Dhanasi, Malasi, Ramakeri and likewise Sindhura,
Ashavari and Bhairavi — these are dear to Malava.

2753Velavali, Pravara, Kanadi and likewise Madhavi,
Kodi and Kedarika — these are dear to Mallara.

2754Velapari, Gauri, Gandhari and likewise Subhaga,
Kaumari and Vairati — these are dear to the raga Shri.

2755Todi, Panchami, Lalita, Patha-manjari,
Gurjari and Vibhasha — these are dear to Vasanta.

2756Mayuri, Dipika, Deshakari and Pahada,
Varadi and Marahatta — these are the wives of Hindola.

2757Natika, then Bhupali, Ramakeri and likewise Gada,
Kamodi, then Kalyani — these are dear to Karnata.

2758Thus the learned speak in various ways;
this is reconciled by the fact that different kalpas are meant.

2759In different lands the ragas bear different names;
no one can give an [exact] determination of the ragas.

2760Thus [it is said]:
The truth of the ragas, which bear different names in different lands,
no one can determine — neither with the vina, nor I.675

2761The knowers of music determine three kinds of ragas:
sampurna, shadava and audava — these three.676

2762Thus [it is said]:
Among them, sampurna, shadava and audava — thus those ragas are threefold.

2763Among them, the sampurna:
The ragas that are sung with seven svaras
the knowers of song call sampurna.

2764Thus [it is said]:
Among them, the sampurna are those that are born from seven svaras.

2765Those with seven svaras are "sampurna": these ragas are called full;
there are many — the raga Shri, Nata, Karnata and others.

2766Thus [it is said]:
These — the raga Shri, Nata, Karnata, Gupta-vasantaka,
Shuddha-bhairava, Vangala, the raga Soma, Amra-panchama,

2767Kamoda, the raga Megha and likewise Dravida-gaudaka,
Varati, Gurjari, Todi, Malavashri and Saindhavi

2768(Malavashri means Malasi, Saindhavi means Sindhuda),
Devakri, Ramakri and likewise Prathama-manjari,
Nata, Velavali, Gauri and others are held to be sampurna.
(By the words "and others" other [ragas] too, Nata and the rest, are included.)

2769This is stated in the Sangita-sara:
Nata, Ghantarava, Natta-narayanaka and Bhupati,
and also Shankarabharana — these are held to be full ragas.677

2770The fruit of singing these sampurna ragas is immense;
this is known everywhere; [so] the knowers of music determine.

2771Thus [it is said] in the Kohaliya:678
Long life, dharma, fame, renown, intelligence, happiness and wealth,
increase of the kingdom, offspring — arise from the full ragas.

2772The forms of the ragas sampurna and the rest, the kinds of rasa and the rest —
what can be said? All this is [set forth] at length in the shastras.

2773Among the sampurna and the rest, certain ragas some sing
the other way round; by the difference of kalpas that too is true.

2774Now [it is told] of the shadava:
All the ragas that arise from six svaras
the knowers of music call shadava.

2775Thus [it is said]:
The ragas that arise from six svaras are called shadava.

2776Gauda, Karnata-gauda and other ragas are among the shadava;
the knowers of sangita say that in singing them there is much fruit.

2777Thus [it is said]:
Gauda, Karnata-gauda, Deshi, and likewise Dhannasika,
Kolahala, Ballali, Desha, Ashavari, and likewise679

2778Khambavati, Harshapuri, Mallari, then Hunchika —
these and others are declared shadava, in the opinion of Harinayaka.680

2779By the words "and others," others too are included — Shrikantha and the rest. As it is said in the Sangita-sara:
Shrikantha, and also Bhauli, Tara, Shalaga, Gaudaka,
Shuddha-abhiri, Madhukari, Chhaya and Nilotpala —
so in the enumeration of the shadava.681

2780Kohala tells the fruit:
Valour in battle, beauty, loveliness, the praise of one's virtues
[come from] singing the shadava ragas — so the ancient sages have declared.

2781Now the audava.
The ragas that arise from five svaras are audava;
the wise name many ragas among the audava.682

2782Thus [it is said]:
Those which are born of five svaras are known as audava.

2783Madhyamadi, Mallara and other ragas are among the audava;
much fruit is gained in this audava singing.

2784Thus [it is said]:
Madhyamadi, Mallara, Deshapala, Malava,
Hindola, Bhairava, Nagadhvani, and likewise Gondakriti,

2785then Lalita, Chhaya, Todi, and likewise Velavali;
Saindhavi with "Pratapa" before it is named, and likewise the second;
these and others are declared audava — ragas that captivate people's hearts.683

2786By the words "and others," Turushka, Gauda and the rest are also included. As it is said in the Sangita-sara in the enumeration of the audava: Turushka, Gauda, Gandhara, Pulinda, Megharanjaka — so.684

2787Kohala tells the fruit:
To destroy disease, to destroy enemies, to dispel fear and grief,
and in rites for pacifying the planets, the audava should be sung.

2788Now the sankirna.
The ragas that have been described, through mutual mixing,
the wise call sankirna; in them is beauty for the ear.685

2789On this Harinayaka [says]:
From the mutual mixing of these ragas [arise] a great many names;
some of them, beautiful to the ear, are called sankirna.

2790Pauravi, Kalyani and others are called sankirna;
the meaning of "sankirna" is: made of the union of two, three or more ragas.

2791Here, Pauravi.
From parts of Deshi and Mallari [comes the raga] that bears the name Pauravi;
thus the wise reveal these easily grasped ragas.

2792Thus [it is said]:
From parts of [the raga] called Desha and of Mallarika
arises this Pauravi — so it is taught.

2793Kalyani:
From [the ragas] called Varati, Nata and Karnataka
arose this charming [raga] called Kalyanika.

2794Saranga:
Saranga arises from Todi and Dhannasika.

2795Gauri:
From the raga Shri and the raga Gauda arises Gauri.

2796Nata-mallarika:
Born of parts of Nata and Mallaraka
is Nata-mallarika.

2797Vallavi:
From the union of Desha and Ashavari, it is declared, [arises] Vallavi.

2798Karnatika:
From parts of Karnata and Bhairava
[arises the raga] called Karnatika, [sung] with a quiver of the voice.

2799Mukhavari:
From the union of Saindhavi and Todika arose Mukhavari.686

2800Ashavari:
From the union of Mallara, Saindhavi and Todi arises Ashavari.

2801Ramakeli:
From the union of Gurjari and Deshika was born Ramakeli.

2802There are many other ragas too with the marks of sankirna;
as each is heard in [a given] land, so the wise should know it.

2803The times at which each of these ragas is fit to be sung —
all those times are stated in the shastras of sangita.

2804Singing out of [its] time is a fault in the singer;
singing the raga Gurjari and the like destroys that fault.

2805Thus [it is said]:
Transgressing the [proper] time in singing surely brings ruin to all;
[but] in group singing, at the king's command and on the stage it brings no fault.687

2806And those who, out of greed and delusion, or in separation, sing [out of time] —
their fault, it is said, the sweet Gurjari destroys.

2807Vasanta, Ramakeli, Gurjari — these three:
singing [them] at any time gives rise to no fault.

2808Thus [it is said] in the Ratna-mala:
Vasanta, Ramakeli, and also the sweet Gurjari —
[when] they are sung at any time, no fault whatever arises.

2809Narada, however, states a particular rule:
At night, after ten dandas have passed, the singing of all [ragas] is enjoined.688

2810All these ragas, taking on form, attentively
consider themselves blessed in the rasa-mandala.

2811What shall I say, O Srinivasa! In the Sri rasa-mandala,
from the singing of various ragas an ocean of joy surges up.

2812This singing has no equal in all the world;
supreme, wondrous nectar [they] shower upon one another.

2813Krishna, gazing at the lotus face of Rai,
reveals in song so much wondrous skill!

2814The characteristics of song were partly stated before;
now learn how the kinds of song were revealed.

2815Song is of two kinds — anibaddha and nibaddha;
anibaddha, as it is defined, has the form of the alapa of a raga.689

2816Song devoid of bandha is anibaddha;
the alapa of a raga is said to be the manifesting of the raga.

2817Thus [it is said]:
Song, it is declared, is twofold: anibaddha and nibaddha;
alapti is without bandha; it has the form of the alapa of a raga.

2818On this it is said:
Because alapti is devoid of bandha, it is called anibaddha.

2819"The alapa of a raga" means its manifesting.

2820Varnalankara in alapa is of two kinds:
one is "a-ta-na-ri," the other "sa-ri-ga-ma" and the rest.690

2821These four [syllables] "a-ta-na-ri" are merely hunkara;
in order they denote Hari, Gauri, Hara and Brahma.691

2822Thus [it is said] in the Narada-samhita and other [books]:
As from hunkara the Veda is born — in the form of "Om,"
[so here]: by the word "ta" Gauri is meant, by the word "na" Hara is meant;
the sounds "ta-na" rise gradually from the hunkara.

2823And there too:
By the sound "a" Hari is designated, by the sound "ri" the Grandsire;
in the word "a-ta-na-ri" is the manifestation of them all.

2824Sa, ri, ga, ma, pa, dha, ni — the seven varnalankaras;
the svaras beginning with shadja — this is varnalapa; so it is known.

2825In alapa the places of the gamakas are exceedingly varied;
in it are many charming nuances — this is well known.692

2826All that [is sung] without tala enters into alapa;
the knowers of song name countless kinds of alapa.

2827Harinayaka, however, [says]:
Joined with varnalankaras, adorned with the places of the gamakas,
charming with many nuances — [such] is called alapti by the knowers.

2828By this [it is meant] that all that [is sung] without tala enters into alapa. Varnalankara, moreover, is meaningless sounds such as hunkara, and the varnalankara "sa-ri-ga-ma" and so on, named in [the teaching of] sangita.

2829The kinds of alapti are many; for fear of prolixity they are not stated.

2830O Srinivasa! In the midst of the Sri rasa-mandali
all perform alapa in countless ways.

2831Whom would that alapa not astonish?
What is the paltry kokila before the sound of those voices!

2832At the time of alapa there is wondrous play:
each displays their own skill.

2833Krishna, the crest-jewel of rasikas, performs alapa on the flute;
He intoxicates the world — what can it be compared to?

2834On the vina the Queen of Vrindavana performs alapa;
who can describe the sweetness of Her alapa?693

2835Lalita and the other sakhis perform alapa on various instruments;
what to speak of others — hearing it, stone melts.

2836Who could tell of the alapa with one mouth?
It surges up like the waves of an ocean of nectar.

2837Immersed in anibaddha singing, they with one another
perform nibaddha song in various ways.

2838Now nibaddha is described.
When [song] is bound by dhatus and angas, it is called nibaddha;
nibaddha is these three: shuddha, chhayalaga, kshudra.694

2839Thus [it is said]:
That which is bound by dhatus and angas is called nibaddha;
and it is held to be threefold: shuddha, chhayalaga, kshudra.

2840Here shuddha is described.
That which is joined with alapa, dhatus and angas is shuddha;
alapa here is defined as meaningful words.

2841Thus [it is said]:
That which is joined with alapas, dhatus and angas is called shuddha.
The knowers of the tradition [say] that by "alapas" here meaningful words alone [are meant].

2842Harinayaka, however, says that alapa is the alapti of gamakas devoid of syllables.

2843The three kinds of nibaddha song have been defined;
some name [them] thus: shuddha, salaga, sankirna.695

2844In the Sangita-sara:
By the distinction of shuddha, salaga and sankirna, song is held to be threefold.
Here by the word "sankirna" kshudra alone is meant.

2845For it is said by the same [author]: "And it is threefold: shuddhaka, chhayalaga, kshudraka."

2846Some say: nibaddha song has three names —
prabandha, vastu, rupaka; this is well known.

2847If in it there are four dhatus and six angas,
then [this] excellent construction is called prabandha.696

2848The wise call shuddha song prabandha;
now learn the characteristics of vastu and rupaka.

2849With three dhatus and the rest and with five angas, vastu is defined;
with two dhatus and two angas, it is called rupaka.697

2850[The words] of Harinayaka:698
Nibaddha has three names: prabandha, vastu, rupaka.

2851That composition which is bound with four dhatus, formed with six angas
and excellent is called prabandha.

2852(Thereby it is said that prabandha is shuddha song itself.)
With three and more dhatus and with five angas it is called vastu;
with two dhatus and likewise with two angas it is celebrated as rupaka.

2853Now on dhatu:
The component part (avayava) of a prabandha is defined as dhatu;
know that a particular part is called avayava.699

2854Some say: the dhatus are four — udgrahaka, and
melapaka, dhruva, abhoga — in this order it is established.

2855Udgraha is first, melapaka comes after it,
after that dhruva, at the end abhoga — these are the four.700

2856Thus [it is said]:
The component part of a prabandha is dhatu; it is declared to be fourfold:
udgrahaka, melapaka, dhruva and abhoga — in order.

2857Udgraha is the first part; then, it is taught, melapaka;
after [it] dhruva, [so called] because of its constancy; and abhoga is held to be the last.

2858In defining prabandha some assert thus:
udgraha, dhruva, abhoga — these three are the dhatus.

2859The first line of a song is called udgraha;
dhruva is in the middle, and at the end abhoga is defined.

2860Thus [it is said] in the [Sangita-]shiromani: Udgraha is the first line, as the ancient teachers have said; dhruva, [so called] because of its constancy, is in the middle, and abhoga, it is taught, is the last. "Because of its constancy" means because of its fixedness, [since it] is taken up again and again.701

2861The line that is between dhruva and abhoga
the knowers call the dhatu named antara.

2862Thus it is said by Harinayaka:
Arising between dhruva and abhoga is another dhatu, called antara.

2863In the abhoga come the names of the poet and the hero;
for this reason the knowers of song give [it] the name "abhoga."

2864Thus [it is said]:
In the abhoga is the name of the poet, and likewise the name of the hero.

2865Such as the dhatus in a prabandha are, such is their definition;
the knowers of song display [them] in various songs.

2866An example in a song — [the raga] Patamanjari:702
The full moon has risen in the night,
its rays drive the darkness far away.
The expanse of the bank of the Daughter of the Sun
shines with abundant whiteness. (Udgraha.)

2867Gently, gently blows the fragrant,
cool breeze from Malaya.
Swarms of bees hum densely; how many
cuckoos and parrots call! (Melapaka.)

2868The Youth of Vraja sports:
seeing the sweet charm of the Vrinda forest,
[He] is utterly enraptured. (Dhruva.)

2869Today in the beautiful rasa-mandala, unattainable [even] for the gods, there is great merriment. Taking the flute in [His] hand, [He] touches [it] to [His] lips; joy fills [His] heart.

2870Excellent songs of many kinds, full of Radhika's qualities and deeds, [He] composes; absorbed in singing, [He shows] an incomparable manner that steals all the pride of the Lord of Rati. (Antara.)

2871In the graceful play of [His] lotus eyes [He] pours forth rasa like a cloud [pouring rain]. What shall Ghanashyama tell? Incomparable love has become manifest in the world. (Abhoga.)703

2872Now on the angas:
The dhatus of a prabandha are five — so the shastras determine.
Prabandha song with six angas is current everywhere.704

2873Svara, biruda, pada, tenaka, patha, tala —
with these six angas a song is supremely sweet.705

2874Svara is defined as sa, ri, ga, ma, pa, dha and the rest;
[words] joined with the names of qualities are, in [this] teaching, called biruda.

2875Pada is words that express [meaning]; of this there are many kinds.
Words such as "tena," "tena" are for the sake of auspiciousness.

2876Patha is the syllables born of instruments: "dha," "dha," "dhilanga" and the like;
tala is chachchatputa, yati and the rest, according to the rules.706

2877These six angas the ancient acharyas define;
some name four: words, svara, tala and tena.

2878Thus [it is said]:
The six angas of a prabandha are svara, biruda, pada,
tenaka, patha and tala. The svaras are sa, ri, ga, ma and the rest.

2879That which [serves] to mention qualities is declared to be biruda;
and that which expresses something else is called pada.

2880The word "tena" is tena; it is determined as having the sense of auspiciousness. "Dham dham," "dhuga-dhuga" and the like are the pathas, the multitudes of instrumental syllables.

2881Adi, yati and the rest are the talas; and tala will be described [later].

2882In the Sangita-parijata:
Pada, tala, svara, patha, tena and [what] is called biruda —
these are the six angas of song, named by the wise.

2883Padas are words that express [meaning]; the talas are chachchatputa and the rest;
the svaras are shadja and the rest; patha is a syllable born of an instrument;

2884tena is an auspicious word; biruda is [a word] joined with the names of qualities.

2885The jatis of prabandha are five: medini, nandini,
dipani, pavani, taravali — so says the muni.707

2886[A prabandha] with six angas is named medini, with five angas nandini,
with four angas dipani, and this one, with three angas, pavani.

2887With two angas it is taravali, say the knowers of song.
Hence know: a prabandha with one anga is not accepted.

2888Thus [it is said]:
The jatis of prabandhas are five, approved by the sages:
medini, nandini, dipani, and also pavani

2889and taravali. Now their characteristics are set forth:
medini is said to have six angas, nandini five,

2890dipani has four angas, pavani is held to have three,
taravali, as the ancient knowers of song have said, has two.
(By this it is established that there is no prabandha with one anga.)

2891In the Sangita-parijata:
The jatis of prabandhas are five, and they [follow] in order:
with six angas there is medini, with five nandini;

2892with four it is called dipani, with three angas pavani;
with two angas the jati taravali arises.

2893The varieties of shuddha prabandha have no end;
the knowers of sangita define [them] in various ways.

2894Thus [it is said]:
Because of the endlessness of shuddha prabandhas, their variety is indeed only one.

2895Even so:
with one tala, with two instruments, with three or with many,
a good poet may certainly compose prabandhas as he wishes.708

2896Moreover:
prabandhas with many talas are to be composed with many ragas
or with one raga — according to the rules for patha and the rest.

2897Their varieties are very many; who will tell of them completely?

2898Therefore it is said:
Neither to ragas, nor to talas, nor, especially, to instruments,
nor even to prabandha songs is there an end in the world.

2899O Srinivasa! Krishna with His beloveds in the rasa dance
reveals shuddha prabandha, unattainable for Brahma and the others.

2900Seeing the beauty of Rai and Kanu, absorbed in song,
Vrinda-devi in her bliss cannot restrain her heart.

2901[She] bids the shukas, sharis and cuckoos
to describe the glory of the qualities of Sri Krishna and Radhika.709

2902At Vrinda's bidding the delighted shukas, sharis and cuckoos
describe the qualities of Sri Krishna and Radhika.

2903The shuka says — an example of a medini song with six angas:
Glory, glory! Delighter of the people, lotus-eyed,
the young nagara like dense collyrium, e e!
Taker of family fidelity from the noble [wives] of Gokula,
moon-faced, ocean of virtues, e e!

2904Son of Nanda, ornament of Vraja, full of rasa,
with charming arms, increaser of joy, e e!
Treasure of the heart of the daughter of Sri Vrishabhanu,
crusher of the pride of myriads of Madanas, e e!

2905Skilled in song, delighting in the ways of Nidhuvana,
incomparable master of the tandava dance, e e!
In the expanse of the courtyard — the bank of the Daughter of the Sun —
adorned with jewels, the hosts of lovely women, e e!

2906Holder of the flute, holder of the mountain, with graceful
red lips, beautiful, e e!
With teeth [like] kunda jasmine, charming, slender-waisted,
the Purandara of the Vrinda forest, e e!

2907Krishna, the foremost champion of love-quarrels,
dha dha dhi dhi ta ga dhenna e e!
Sa sa ri ga ri — the Lord of Narahari,
e i a iti ai ai atenna e e!

2908The shari says — an example of a medini song:
Glory! Worshipped by the world, the renowned princess,
Radhika, moon-faced, dispeller of sorrow!
Delighter of Shyama's heart, breaker of [His] firm composure,
with doe's eyes that put to shame the lotus, the khanjana and the fish!

2909Whose luster has conquered the lightning, supremely charming, the beautiful lady,
crusher of the pride of the Daughter of the Ocean and others,
with a lovely gentle smile, with graceful sweet speech, enchantress of the world,
increaser of the joy of Lalita and the others!710

2910Lovely in the adornment of love, [in] pastimes ever new and new,
the delight of the Vrinda forest, with an elephant's gait,
rapt in the rasa of the rasa dance, a river of sweetness,
the jewel of all women, the mistress of Narahari!

2911Jhanta jham jhanta takha vitakato thunna drimiki
trigao takata ta thaiya.
Sari rigama pamaga manma gari sas sati ai
tenna tenna tenam ti ai e a.711

2912The cuckoo says — an example of a nandini song with five angas:
Glory, glory, Krishna, merciful Keshava,
lotus-eyed, delighter of the people, a!
Elephant in the lotus forest of young maidens, charming
khanjana in the cage of the beloved's heart, a!

2913With a sweet smile on the lovely moon of the face,
breaker of the weight of Radha's composure, a!
Beautiful, best of dancers, son of Nanda,
collyrium for the eyes of ever new young maidens, a!

2914Sari gama gama pama manmama garisa
tenna tennati ati ai iya.
Ai, increaser of Narahari's joy, e e,
ai ati ai tiya.

2915O Srinivasa! The birds in various ways
sing the fair fame of Radha and Krishna in shuddha songs.

2916The varieties of song prabandhas cannot be told;
the shastras define [them] by shakti, varna, particular features and the rest.712

2917Ela and the rest are difficult; among them are twenty-six songs;
what is easy and what is hard in this the shastras have revealed.713

2918The first is named Panchataleshvara;
after it come four varieties of Varnasvara:

2919Varnasvara beginning with svara, Varnasvara beginning with patha,
Varnasvara beginning with pada, Varnasvara beginning with tena.

2920Next they name the song Svarartha-matrika.
Thus the knowers of song define the twenty-six.

2921Thus [it is said]:
There are difficult prabandhas — Ela and the rest — spoken of by the sages;
of them twenty-six are named by the learned Harinayaka.

2922And they are listed in order, by name alone:
Panchataleshvara, Varnasvara and Angacharini,714

2923and also Svarartha-matrika, Ragakadambaka,
Svaradya-karana, then Vartani, and likewise Talarnava,

2924Shriranga, Shrivilasa, then Panchabhangi,
Panchanana, Matilaka, and also Simhanila.

2925Tribhangi, Hamsanila, and also Harivilasaka,
Sudarshana, Svaranga, Shrivardhana, Harshavardhana,

2926Vira, Shrimangala, and Lahadi is also named;
[the prabandha] called by the name Navaratna is named, and also Sarabhanilaka,715

2927and the one that is called Kanthabharana: these are held to be the twenty-six.
There are also six others — Chandraprakashaka and the rest.

2928The characteristics of all these prabandhas are well known;
the poets describe [them] so that all hearts are delighted.

2929At Vrinda's bidding the bee, with great eagerness,
sings a svarartha prabandha in the guise of humming.

2930The syllables of the svarartha prabandha are sa, ri, ga, ma and the rest;
in two kinds, shuddha and mishra, [it] expresses [meaning] at will.716

2931Thus [it is said]:
Where the desired meaning is expressed by the syllables of the svaras alone,
that [prabandha] is svarartha; it is twofold, by the distinction of shuddha and mishra.
(If by the syllables of the svaras — sa, ri, ga, ma, pa, dha, ni — the desired meaning is expressed at will, then it is svarartha: such is the sense.)

2932Joyfully the bee reveals the svarartha prabandha;
hearing [it], Sri Lalita and the other sakhis are filled with happiness.

2933For example — the raga Kedara:717
Glory! Crown of rasikas, Krishna, tender-limbed,
shining like dense collyrium!
With the moon of [Your] face anointed with the nectar of smiles,
making the directions clear with lovely rays!

2934With charming wide eyes that have conquered the lotus,
stealer of the wealth of the young maidens' composure!
Triumphant in Vraja, the young crown prince, the best of dancers,
holder of the flute, with reddish lips!

2935Crusher of the pride of the Lord of Rati, enjoyer of the sweet rasa dance,
beautiful, incomparable!
Graceful, like a jewel, greedily drawn to the fragrance
of the lotus faces of the jewels among the women of Vraja!718

2936King of the new kunjas, subduer of the serpent,
in charming attire of every kind!
Increaser of Ghanashyama's joy — pama gamamma gari
mapa dhani padha nidha!719

2937Thus Vrinda directs a multitude of birds;
with songs of various prabandhas they all give delight.

2938O Srinivasa! Krishna with His beloveds in the rasa dance
reveals the highest limit of the prabandhas of shuddha song.

2939Within shuddha some speak of shuda prabandha;
others reveal shuda within chhayalaga.720

2940Now, chhayalaga:
Because [it] clings to the shadow of shuddha, it is called "chhayalaga";
in it shuda is composed with talas, instruments and the rest.

2941The weaving together of many talas — such is the charming shuda;
the term "chhayalaga" has another name, salaga.721

2942Thus [it is said]:
That which clings to the shadow of shuddha they know as chhayalaga;
it is charming, composed as shuda with talas, instruments and the rest.
(Shuda is the weaving together of many talas in one: such is the sense. By the words "clings to the shadow" it is said that it arises with some of the characteristics of shuddha: such is the sense.)

2943It is said of this:
If [in it] there is only a shadow of the features stated [above],
it is to be known as chhayalaga — [so say] the munis Bharata and the others.

2944(It also has another name, salaga: such is the sense.) Of this Harinayaka has said: Now, the shuda that [is] chhayalaga is itself salaga.

2945According to differing views the salaga shudas are many;
and so they define dhruvaka and the rest [as] excellent.

2946Thus [it is said] in Damodara and in the Panchama-sara-samhita:
Dhruvaka, manthaka, pratimantha, nisharuka,
vasaka, pratitala, and also ekatalika,
yati and jhumari — thus is the salaga shuda named.722

2947[Now] the varieties of dhruvaka and the rest are told:
Dhruvakas are said to be sixteen, manthakas of six kinds,
pratimanthas five, nisharukas are known to be seven;

2948vasakas are said to be four, pratitalakas four,
ekatali of three kinds, yatis are held to be four;

2949and jhumari is only one: these are the salagas named.

2950Some say there are ten other salagas — charcharika and the rest;
thus they, the salagas, come to be nineteen — a multitude.723

2951The characteristics of dhruvaka and the rest are extremely difficult;
shuda in nine talas — it gives joy in every way.

2952Thus [it is said]:
Adi, yati, nasaru, and also addatala, triputa,
rupaka, jhampaka, mantha, ekatali — so [the talas] are named.724

2953That which is composed with these nine talas is called shuda;
such a shuda is charming in singing, in playing instruments and in dance.

2954The varieties of prabandhas — shuda and the rest — are manifold;
their characteristics, examples and so on are set forth in the shastras.

2955In song tala is joined; without tala there is no purity —
as it is with a boat without a helmsman.

2956The derivation of the word "tala" [is explained] in many ways;
the acharyas have made this known.

2957Thus [it is said]:
Without tala the purity of song does not arise in song and the rest,
as with a boat without a helmsman; therefore we set them forth.725

2958Here the acharyas have explained the derivation of the word "tala" in many ways.

2959Harinayaka [says] of this:
Because by the evenness of time and, moreover, by its charm
it establishes sangita, it is called tala.
("Talayati" — establishes; the root "tal" is in the sense of "establishing.")

2960But in the Sangita-sara:
"Ta" is Isha, Girija is "la";
hence tala, from the union of Shiva and Shakti.
Or else here "tala" is from the root "tal" with [the suffix] ghañ;
or "tala" is from the union of "ta" and "la."726

2961In the Ratna-mala:
"Ta" is Sharajanma, "a" is called Vishnu,
"la" is declared to be Maruta: these gods dwell in the tala.727

2962But Vachaspati [says]:
The action — stretching and bending of the fingers of the hand and the rest —
and the measure of time [set] by it is here called tala.728

2963Now [it is told] of the talas:
The talas chachchatputa, chachaputa and the rest are the chief ones;
a hundred and one talas — [this] is accepted everywhere.

2964Thus [it is said]:
Chachchatputa, chachaputa, and also shatpitaputraka,
sampakveshtaka, udghatta, aditala and darpana,729

2965charchari, simhanila, kandarpa, simhavikrama,
shriranga, ranganila, rangatala, parikrama,

2966pratyanga, gajalila, tribhinna, viravikrama,
hamsanila, varnanila, and also rajachudamani,

2967rangadyota, rajatala, and also simhavikridita,
vanamali, varnatala, mishra, rangapradipaka,

2968hamsanada, simhanada, the one called mallikamoda,
then sharabhalila and rangabharana,

2969then turagalila, and after it simhanandana,
jayashri, vijayananda, pratitala, dvitiyaka,

2970makaranda, kirtitala, vijaya, jayamangala,
rajavidyadhara, mantha, jayatala, sudurbala,730

2971then nihsharuka, krida, tribhangi, kokilapriya,
shrikanta, bindumali, samatala and nandana,

2972udikshana, mallika, dhenkika, varnamanthika,
abhinanda, antarakrida, laghutala and dipaka,

2973anangatala, vishama, sandikunda and mukundaka,
ekatali, kankala, chatustala and khamkhudi,731

2974abhanga, rajavankara, and also laghushekhara,
and another, pratapashekhara, jagajhampa, chaturmukha,

2975vankara, pratimantha, and also the tala tritiyaka;
after it, as should be known, vasanta, lalita, shiva,

2975akarashakha, shattala, vardhana, and also vardhaka;
then, as the learned declare, rajanarayana;
madana too should be known, and also parvatilochana.732

2976Then there is sarangatala, then shrinandivardhana,
and another, lilavilokita, and also lalitapriya,

2977janaka, lakshmisha, the one called ragavardhana,
and utsava: thus the talas are one more than a hundred.

2978In Damodara and others some of these are found otherwise;
since the opinions of the rishis are many, what harm is there in variants among them?

2979The characteristics and examples of all these talas
the knowers of sangita have joyfully made known.

2980The angas of tala are fivefold, beginning with anudruta, [they] say,
and they define the rules: [how many] matras in laghu and the rest.733

2981Thus [it is said]:
Anudruta, druta, laghu, and after it guru
and pluta: thus in order the angas of tala are fivefold.
Apart from anudruta, the names of the others are [from the syllables] da, la, ga, pa.

2982Laghu is of one matra, guru of two matras,
pluta of three matras, druta of half a matra,
and anudruta of half of druta's matra,
and its name may also be "virama."

2983Anudruta, druta, laghu, guru, pluta — such are the signs.
(The signs are these: …)734

2984[Now] the places of their strokes, with [their] measure, are told:735
Druta is a stroke of the hand [from a height of] four fingers;
la, ga, pa — eight, sixteen, twenty-four.

2985Thus [it is said]:
For [the stroke] called druta the height is said to be four fingers.736
("Uchchhrita" means "high.")
Laghu is declared to be of eight fingers, guru is of sixteen fingers,
and pluta of three times eight fingers; and druta is a slight movement of the hand.737

2986Now [it is told] of the ways of marking them:
Tala is marked in two ways: with sound and without sound;
in guru, pluta and the rest a soundless [stroke] is needed.738

2987Tala: in guru, one sounded, one soundless;
in pluta, one sounded, two soundless; in anudruta,739

2988laghu and druta the tala is without soundless [strokes].
With a loud stroke of the hand the tala is called sounded.

2989Thus [it is said]:
The marking of tala is twofold: with sound and without sound.
A loud stroke is sounded; laghu has only one [stroke].

2990For guru a double stroke is declared: one is sound, the other soundless;
and [the stroke] that goes to half — from half the sound of laghu — [is called] druta.740

2991In pluta there is one sounded stroke, then two strokes;
they are soundless: one [is made] upward, and the other downward.

2992To the varieties of tala there is no end;
in the Sri rasa-mandala they all became embodied.

2993Krishna, joining both hands in a sweet curve,
keeps the tala thus — with what can it be compared?

2994Sri Radhika, displaying a wondrous grace,
joins hand to hand, smiling slightly.

2995The wonder that arises in the blending of the sounds
of the strokes of the hands, the bracelets and the rest — who will describe it?

2996Strokes of the hands in many ways, many talas in the songs —
Lakshmi and the others are amazed: with what can it be compared?

2997All of Radhika's companions are wonderful:
one in one tala, another in another, reveals songs.

2998Singing in chhayalaga is extremely difficult;
the lovely Lalita joyfully reveals it.

2999Krishna, supremely fond of play, to Lalita and the others
gave leave to sing kshudra songs.

3000Now [it is told] of kshudra song:
Mere words joined with tala and dhatu are kshudra song;
the dhatus are udgraha and the rest, described before, as is fitting.

3001Thus [it is said]:
Mere words joined with tala and dhatu are called kshudra.

3002A kshudra song is for the most part like shuddha and salaga;
consonance at the ends [of the lines] in it the shastras call praiseworthy.

3003The kinds of kshudra song are four: chitrapada, and also
chitrakala, dhruvapada, panchali — [so] it is known.741

3004Thus [it is said]:
It is indeed fourfold: among them chitrapada is the first,
[then] chitrakala, dhruvapada and panchali — by their distinctions.

3005The characteristics of these songs are very extensive.
By the variety of its padas the [song] called chitrapada is known.742

3006Thus [it is said]:
Where variety is seen in the padas alone,
and there is no variety in dhatu and the rest, know that as chitrapada.
(Variety of padas, moreover, is the possession of qualities: gentle consonance, clarity and the rest.)
Such is chitrapada.

3007Now, chitrakala:
Chitrakala: in the dhruva the matras are fewer, in the other [parts] equal;
from three to eight lines — such is the rule of this song.743

3008Thus [it is said]:
If in the udgraha and abhoga the matras are equal, but in the dhruva fewer,
[and the song] is rich in lines — from three up to eight — know: that is chitrakala.

3009The characteristics of dhruvapada and the rest are known everywhere.
In the vernacular and in Sanskrit they sing many kinds of songs.

3010Songs in Sanskrit, in the vernacular and others are well known;
the knowers of sangita define [their] kinds: divya and the rest.744

3011This is said:
Song is divya, manusha, and also divya-manusha.
Divya is composed in Sanskrit, manusha arises from Prakrit;

3012that arising from Sanskrit and Prakrit is called divya-manusha.
And some consider as manusha [a song] in a language that arose in a particular country.

3013Anga, Vanga, Kalinga and other [countries] are the sources of regional languages and the rest.
In whatever countries whatever languages are cherished,
those, taken from the speech of the people there, one should employ [in song].745

3014Some define the particulars of the composition of song and the rest:
three varieties, named sama, ardhasama and vishama.746

3015Thus [it is said] in Kohala:
Song is threefold: sama, ardhasama and vishama.
With four lines of equal number of matras [it] is called sama.

3016The song whose first and third lines are equal, and the second and fourth equal too, is named ardhasama.

3017If all four lines of [a song] differ in their number of matras,
that song the sages Bharata and the others call vishama.

3018What further particulars there are in song — what do others know of that?
In the pastimes of the Sri rasa Krishna reveals everything.

3019At the singing of the sakhis Krishna, rejoicing at heart,
praising [them] much, embraces the sakhis.

3020From the embrace of the sakhis comes Radhika's great happiness.
What do others know of the delight that grows in song?

3021What can be said — the qualities of song are of many kinds,
all those that shine in the Sri rasa-mandala.

3022Now, the qualities of song:
The qualities of song the knowers of song have proclaimed:
graha, laya, yati, variety of mana,747

3023repetition of dhatu, and also newness,
manifold meaning of the matu words, pleasingness of the raga,

3024gamaka, clarity of meaning, the charming
combination of tenna, patha and svara in various ways.

3025Know: these are the qualities of song — graha and the rest, nine;
in this there are further varieties of many kinds.748

3026Thus [it is said]:
Now the qualities of song: graha, laya and yati, variety of mana;
repetition of dhatu and newness, manifold meaning
of matu, pleasingness of the raga, then gamaka, clarity of meaning,
and the combination of tennas, svara and patha in various ways.

3027Moreover:
Of all these qualities the most necessary is this:
the inclusion of speech possessed of excellences, ornaments and rasa.

3028Graha and the rest — all the qualities that [here] are defined —
the wise expound in many ways.

3029Among them, on graha:
Graha is anagata, sama, atita — these three;
anagata graha and the rest — such are the three names.749

3030Thus [it is said]:
Tala makes the course of song even; its grahas are three,
named anagata, sama and atita — so it is held everywhere.

3031On anagata:
When the tala is taken before the beginning of the song,
all call this the anagata graha.

3032Thus [it is said]:
When before the beginning of the song two syllables are uttered
[and then] the tala is set, this is called anagata graha.

3033(The meaning here is this: the syllable taken in excess at the beginning of the song is "anagata": it never enters within the tala.)

3034On sama:
If tala and song arise at the same time,
then the wise call it the sama graha.

3035Thus [it is said]:
When the tala coincides [with the song] from the very utterance of the song,
then, because they arise at one time, this is called sama graha.

3036So also the atita graha; its kinds are many:
the knowers of sangita have set [them] forth in various ways.

3037Thus [it is said]:
If the kala that will fall later is placed at the beginning
and [thus] the tala is sung, then this is called tala graha.750

3038Now, laya:
Laya — [when] the evenness of the actions of graha and the rest is manifest;
it has three kinds: druta, vilambita, madhya.751

3039Thus [it is said]:
