The mutual evenness of the actions — of song, instruments and the placing of steps —
or else [the evenness] of action and tala: this the wise call laya.
So [says] Vachaspati.752

3040Harinayaka, however, [says]: "The pause between actions is called laya."
The wise have called it threefold: druta, madhya and vilambita.

3041Druta is of one matra; madhya has a pause twice [that of] druta;
vilambita is double [madhya]; all of these belong to all the talas.

3042Some by this define tala;
but in all views laya is a particular form of singing.

3043On yati:
The rule for carrying the laya is yati;
its three kinds: srotovaha, sama, gopuchchhika.753

3044In these three particular [kinds] of pause are defined;
this the wise expound in many ways.

3045Thus [it is said]:
Yati is indeed the rule for carrying the laya;
it is threefold: srotovaha, sama and gopuchchhika.

3046Srotovaha, sama, gopuchchhika — the three [kinds] of laya;
[their] characteristics are easy; know: the shastras expound [them].

3047On mana:
The action of the tala that gives a pause is called mana;
one avarta bears the name vardhamana,

3048the second avarta is hiyamana — [so] it is determined;
the characteristics of these two, know, are known [as] easy.754

3049Thus [it is said]:
The action of the tala that gives a pause is here called mana;
since it gives the tala a pause, mana completes the tala.

3050If it falls on the second kala in the dhruva, then
the avarta in the tala is called vardhamana — so the knowers of tala hold.

3051But if the mana falls on the last kala in the dhruva, then
the avarta is called hiyamana — so the wise have said.

3052Now, repetition of dhatu:
The way of repetition of dhatu the worthy describe:
the parts of the song are sung again and again — anew.

3053Manifold meaning of the matu words:
The manifold meaning of the matu words they define thus:
in a turn of speech of one [and the same] sense [words] are not used.

3054The characteristics of dhatu and matu [I] have made known before;
since [it is] easy, there was no detailed account.

3055On the pleasingness of the raga:
The evident pleasingness of the raga destroys many sorrows;
the knowers of raga reveal [its] qualities: being pleasant to the ear and the rest.

3056Thus [it is said]:
Pleasant to the ear, abiding in yati, with angas, bringing happiness,
rich in [the registers] mandra, madhya and tara — [such is] the desired pleasingness of a raga.

3057On gamaka:
The nature of gamaka is the vibration of a svara;
in the hearts of the listeners it gives rise to great happiness.

3058The kinds of gamaka are fifteen;
the characteristics of all, in order, beginning with tiripa, are set forth.

3059Thus [it is said]:
The vibration of a svara, bringing happiness to the listener's heart, is gamaka.
Its varieties are tiripa, sphurita, and also kampita,

3060nila, andolita, vali, tribhinna, kuvala, ahata,
unnamita, plavita, hunkrita, and also mudrita,
namita and mishrita — thus fifteen are named.755

3061Now [it is told] of their characteristics:
Lovely in its imitation of the lightest vibration of the sound of the damaru,
with a speed of a quarter of a druta — [the gamaka] is called tiripa.756

3062With a speed made of a third of a druta, [the gamaka] is held to be sphurita;
with singing at half the measure of a druta, [the gamaka] is called kampita.

3063Nila is with the speed of a druta, andolita with the speed of a laghu;
vali is joined with various curves — as the raga [requires].

3064Tribhinna is a dense sound without pauses in the three registers;
kuvala is that same vali, knotted, soft to the throat.

3065Ahata is when, striking the svara ahead, one turns back;
unnamita is said to be that which to svaras higher and higher

3066passes in order; plavita is a vibration in prolonged singing;
hunkrita is held to be [the gamaka] filled with a charming sound "hum."757

3067Mudrita is the gamaka born of closed lips;
namita — so the knowers of sound call [the gamaka] from the lowering of the svaras.

3068From the mixing of these comes mishrita; it has numerous varieties;
I have not named them, since they are unfit for use and unknowable.

3069The way of practising this:
At night in the months of Magha and Pausha, only in the last watch,
standing in water, the practitioner should master these gamakas.758

3069aThese are the fifteen kinds of gamaka;
some, by the distinction of the seven svaras, name seven kinds.759

3069bThus [it is said]:
The vibration of a svara is gamaka; by the distinction of the svaras it is sevenfold.
(The meaning is this: by the distinction of the seven svaras there are seven kinds. This, moreover, is seen in the Narada-samhita.)

3070Now, clarity of meaning:
When on utterance all in the words is understood,
a faultless meaning full of rasa is called clarity.

3071Thus [it is said]:
When on the utterance of speech the meaning is fully grasped,
[and] the meaning is pleasant, faultless and with rasa — that indeed is clarity of meaning.

3072The placing of tena, patha and svara with variety:
tena is used after patha and svara, and never at the beginning.

3073What fault arises in song from the absence of the qualities and the rest —
of that know something; this the knowers of song expound at length.

3074Without tala — illness, without dhatu — loss of wealth;
a song without dhatu, matu and pada is an enemy.

3075Thus [it is said]:
Without tala — illness of the body, without dhatu — loss of wealth;
where there are no dhatu, matu and pada, that song is an enemy.

3076Now [it is told] of the faults of song:
Some say the faults of song are of many kinds;
others define [them] briefly: stumbling of speech and the rest.

3077Thus [it is said]:
The faults in songs are: stumbling of speech and the rest,
composition lacking tala and the rest,
impairment of dhatu, matu and the rest, harsh words,
loss of rasa and the rest, unpleasantness to the ear.

3078Although in songs there are many such and similar faults, they are not named [here]; if [one needs] to grasp them in knowledge, let one look into this and that [in the books].760

3079One who sings a song is called a singer;
the characteristics of a singer are set forth in various ways.

3080[It is told] of the characteristics of a singer:
Singers are of three kinds: the best, the middling, the lowest;
the characteristics of these three the shastras set forth plainly.

3081Thus [it is said]:
A singer is said to be of three kinds: the best, the middling, the lowest.
With a pure-sounding voice, with a good sharira, knowing the distinctions of many ragas,761

3082endowed with graha, mana and laya, knowing tala, having conquered fatigue,
with easy and graceful movement in gamakas touching the three sthanas,762

3083skilled in singing prabandhas, intent on careful performance,
master of his voice, knowing the sthayi, faultless, endowed with [good] retention —

3084[such is] the best. The middling is named [one endowed] with some of these qualities; but one who, though endowed with qualities, is full of faults is called the lowest.

3085There is also [a division] into five kinds — shikshakara and the rest: one skilled in teaching [is called] a shikshakara; thus are known the shikshakara and the others.

3086Thus [it is said]:
Shikshakara, anukara, rasika, and also ranjaka
and bhavaka — thus the knowers of song have called the singer fivefold.

3087One skilled in teaching without omission is held by the virtuous to be a shikshakara; one who imitates the manner of others is called an anukara.

3088One absorbed in rasa is a rasika; one who delights the listeners is a ranjaka;
one who imparts a special excellence to the song is called a bhavaka.

3089The wise further speak of singers of three kinds:
one, two, many — these are the plain characteristics.

3090Thus [it is said]:
The singer is of three kinds: ekala, yamala and vrinda.
One who sings entirely alone is an ekala singer;
one who has a second is a yamala; one who is with a group is a vrinda singer.

3091[It is told] of the faults of a singer:
The faults of a singer are of many kinds:
timidity, indistinct words and the rest are well known in the shastras.

3092Thus [it is said]:
Timid, with indistinct words, shaking his head, puffing, off-key,
with clenched teeth, closing his eyes, and also unsteady in the grama,
singing with a twisted neck, [now] scanty, [now] excessive in svaras, mixing ragas,
with trembling body, inattentive, making [the song] insipid, crow-voiced, hasty.
("Crow" means with a harsh cry.)

3093Moreover:
falling out of tala, stretching the body of the song, frightful in appearance, goat-throated, unsteady,
with puffed-out cheeks, nasal — such indeed is a faulty singer.

3094There are many other faults, not named for fear of prolixity;
these unnamed merits and faults are to be learned from other books.763

3095Ragas, yakara and the rest — however many kinds [there are] —
the knowers of sangita have set this forth at length.764

3096These songs and the rest are transcendental: there is not a trace of fault in them;
in passing I have said a little, [only] to give an indication.

3097Krishna, the Supreme Person, is free from [worldly] merits and faults;
whatever lila He performs captivates everyone.

3098He is a Person not of this world, yet [His] lila is like the world's;
seeing and hearing [it], grass, wood and stone melt.

3099Whoever describes it in whatever way,
freed from the poison of bad association, attains those feet.765

3100O Srinivasa, what shall I say of the delights of the rasa dance!
Krishna reveals all of this together with His beloveds.

3101Nada, shruti, svaras and the rest — however many kinds [there are] —
even Bharata and the other munis find no end to them.

3102That at which Brahma and the others are filled with the greatest wonder —
all such marvels [He] reveals in song.

3103Songs in refined Sanskrit and in the languages of various lands
He sings in all those styles, describing [them].766

3104Now He sings alone, now together with Radhika —
who can describe the manner of singing of Them both?

3105Now together with Lalita and the other sakhis
Radhika and Krishna sing with wondrous modulations.

3106All those sounds of the voice are the essence of nectar;
in them is the wondrous movement of various gamakas.

3107Hearing that singing, no one can remain composed;
there is nothing in the universe to compare it with.

3108As the singing is, so are the various instruments — the greatest wonder;
the sound of the instruments steals away the composure of the three worlds.

3109Now [it is told] of instruments:
Through instruments song and tala [gain] beauty; the instruments are of four [kinds]:
tata, anaddha, shushira and the one called ghana — so the shastras say.767

3110Tata is the vina and the rest, anaddha the muraja and the rest;
the vamshi and the rest are shushira, the kamsya-tala and the rest ghana.

3111Thus [it is said]:
Since without instruments neither song nor tala shines,
therefore here [the teaching on] the auspicious instrument is set forth by us.

3112Tata, anaddha, shushira and ghana — thus [instruments] are of four kinds.
Tata is the instrument vina and the rest, anaddha the muraja and the rest,
the vamshi and the rest are shushira, the kamsya-tala and the rest ghana.

3113In the Sangita-damodara:
Tata, shushira, anaddha, ghana — in this way [instruments] are of four kinds.
Tata is the instrument with strings, shushira the vamsha and the rest,
anaddha is that covered with hide, ghana is held to be the tala and the rest.

3114Of [these] four I make known a little, only the names;
the knowers of sangita reveal the characteristics of the instruments and the rest.

3115Tata, namely:
The tata instruments are the alavani, the brahma-vina, and also
the kinnari, the laghu-kinnari and the rest — so it is known.

3116Thus [it is said] in the Sangita-damodara:
Alavani, brahma-vina, kinnari, laghu-kinnari,
vipanchi, vallaki, jyeshtha, chitra, ghoshavati, jaya,

3117hastika, kubjika, kurma, sarangi, parivadini,
trishari, shatatantri, and also nakulaushthi and kamsari,

3118audumbari, pinaki, nibandha, and also pushkala,
gadavaranahasta, rudra, then svara-mandala,
kavilasa, madhusyandi, ghona and the rest — [these] are tata.768

3119And likewise:
Another vina is the kachchhapi; it is sometimes [called] rupavati.
(That is, this same one is called rupavati.)
("Rudra" is the rudra-vina.)

3120Anaddha, namely:
Know the varieties of anaddha: [the one] called mardala, and also
the muraja, dhakka, pataha and the rest — so it is known.

3121Thus [it is said]:
The mardala, and also the muraja, dhakka, pataha, changava,
panava, kundali, bheri, ghata-vadya and jharjhara,

3122damaru, tamaki, mantha, hudukka, maddu, dindima,
upanga, dardura and the rest — [these] are named anaddha.769

3123The mardala is the best of the anaddha; its name is mridanga;
[it is] of two kinds: made of wood and of clay.

3124This mardala is the best of all instruments; in union with it
all instruments gain beauty — it is known in the shastras.

3125In the mridanga Brahma and the other gods ever reside;
[its sound] is supremely auspicious, captivating everyone.

3126Thus [it is said] in the Sangita-darpana:
Among the anaddha the mardala is the best.770

3127In the Sangita-damodara:
Mridangas are said to be made also of clay.
Thus the mardala is called the very best of all instruments;
having attained union with it, every instrument shines.

3128In the Sangita-parijata:
In the middle part of the mridanga Brahma always dwells;
as the gods abide in his world, so they are present here too;
since the mridanga contains all the gods, it is all-auspicious.

3129The making of the mridanga, the varieties of instruments, [their] characteristics and the rest the knowers of sangita describe in various ways.

3130Some say the varnas arising from the instrument are twenty;
others say something of the fine rules for arranging the varnas.771

3131Thus [it is said] in the Sangita-parijata:
The patha-varnas composed by Umapati are twenty, and so on.772

3132The characteristics of a mridanga player are many:
"steady," "skilled in playing the instrument" and the rest — so some say.

3133Thus [it is said]:
Steady, skilled in playing the instrument, eloquent, clearly bringing out the syllables of the patha,
devoted to the practice of tala, able to display mature mastery in all the gamakas,
skilled in dancing with the turns of varied playing, well versed in the course of the song,
contented, playing with ease, quick-handed — such is the celebrated mridanga player.

3134All this the knowers of sangita have set forth at length.
The varieties of shushira instruments are a true elixir.

3135Now, shushira:
Many varieties of shushira instruments are defined:
the vamshi, pavi, madhuri, tittiri, shankha and the rest.

3136Thus [it is said]:
The vamsha, and also the pavi, madhuri, tittiri, shankha, kahala,
dodahi, murali, bukka, shringika, svaranabhi,

3137the shringa, the lapika-vamsha and, besides, the charma-vamsha —
these varieties of shushira were named by the ancient sages.773

3138The characteristics of what is called the vamsha are many in the shastras:
graceful, straight, free from defects in the joints and the rest.

3139Thus [it is said]:
Graceful, straight, devoid of defects in the joints;
of bamboo, but it may also be of khadira, or of red sandalwood,
("Of bamboo" means a vamsha [of bamboo].)

3140or of white sandalwood, or golden, or made of ivory;
it has an inner bore equal to the little finger — and so on.

3141The length of the vamshika is from six fingers
up to eighteen fingers: such is the view of the shastras.

3142Thus [it is said]:
This vamsha may be of five fingers; with an increase of one finger at a time
it receives the names "of six fingers" and so on — up to eighteen fingers.

3143By their measure in fingers the flutes have many names;
the excellent ones — Mahananda and the rest — the shastras define.774

3144Thus [it is said]:
Mahananda, and also Nanda, Vijaya and Jaya —
these four best vamshas are approved by the muni Matanga.775

3145Of ten fingers is Mahananda, Nanda of eleven fingers,
of the measure of twelve fingers, it is declared, is Vijaya,
of the measure of fourteen fingers is what is called Jaya.

3146The merits, faults and the rest of the flute the wise reveal;
all this is known. [Now] I make known the ghana instruments.

3147Now, ghana:
Among the ghana instruments are the karatala, the kamsya-vala, and also
the jaya-ghanta, the shuktika and the rest — of various kinds.

3148Thus [it is said]:
Karatala, kamsya-vala, jaya-ghanta, and also shuktika,
kampaka, ghata-vadya, ghanta-todya and gharghara,

3149jhanjha-tala, manjira, kartari and uddhura —
these twelve are named by the lord of sages [instruments] called ghana.776

3150The characteristics of the karatala and the rest are set forth in the shastras.
To the tata and other instruments the gods and others have their right.

3151Thus [it is said]:
Tata instruments are for the gods, saushira for the Gandharvas,
anaddha for the Rakshasas, and ghana for men, as is known.777

3152Great good fortune dawned for all these instruments:
in the Sri rasa-mandala an incomparable beauty arose.

3153O Srinivasa! How wondrous is the way of the rasa:
various instruments sound there that enchant Brahma and the others.

3154The son of the king of Vraja, skilled in all instruments,
surrounded by His beloveds, enchants millions of Kandarpas.778

3155He plays the flute — with what wondrous grace!
In the three worlds there is no comparison to give for this beauty.

3156In mandra, madhya and tara — a captivating alapa of svaras;
hearing the sound of the flute, Maheshvara is overwhelmed.

3157Radha, the enchantress of the worlds, the embodiment of rasa,
plays the alavani instrument in the pure manner.779

3158Shadja, madhyama and gandhara — the three gramas:
as they are revealed in song, so She reveals [them] on the instrument.

3159Lalita playfully plays the brahma-vina —
she who is skilled in revealing shrutis and the rest on the instrument.780

3160The beautiful Vishakha, with great sweet grace,
plays the kachchhapi-vina in various manners.

3161The beautiful Suchitra plays the rudra-vina,
gracefully revealing the distinctions of svaras and jatis.

3162Champakalatika joyfully plays the vipanchi,
surpassing all in revealing murchhanas, talas and the rest.

3163Rangadevi gracefully plays the yantraka:
how wondrously the gamakas appear in it!781

3164The beautiful Sudevi joyfully plays the sarangi:
in it the varieties of ragas and the prabandhas are revealed.

3165Tungavidya delightedly plays the kinnari,
pouring a rain of nectar in the Sri rasa-mandala.

3166Indulekha joyfully plays the svara-mandala,
effortlessly revealing the distinctions of svaras.782

3167All the hosts of Sri Radhika's sakhis, as many as there are,
are all absorbed in every way in playing all the instruments.

3168Some play the mardala and the madal in every way,
revealing wondrous talas unheard of in the world.783

3169Some play the muraja and the upanga instrument,
at the sound of which no composure remains in the heart.784

3170Some play the damaru with the utmost skill;
the damaru is dear to Shiva — this is known in the world.

3171Thus [it is said] in the Sangita-parijata:
The damaru, let it be known, is two fists [in size], two-faced, slender in the middle;
its faces, one fist in measure, are covered with fine skin.

3172It is played with two knots on cords attached to it;
this instrument ever shines in the hand of the Lord of Uma.785

3173Some play karatalas and other instruments;
the Sri rasa-mandala is filled with the splendor of the instruments.

3174All the hosts of Sri Radhika's sakhis, as many as there are —
who could tell how lovely they are with their various instruments?

3175The sounds of all the instruments blend into one — how wondrous!
It is as if a rain of nectar falls in the Sri rasa-mandala.

3176The heart of Sri Vrinda-devi is full of great joy:
she supplies wondrous instruments unknown to the shastras.

3177Rai and Kanu, immersed in the rasa of the instruments,
dance with great jubilation in their hearts.

3178Lalita and the other sakhis, in fitting bliss,
dance. I shall make known a little of the varieties [of dance].

3179Now [it is told] of dance:
Nartana, in order, is natya, nritya and nritta — three [kinds];
these three are born of the Vedas — so the knowers of dance define.786

3180Nartana is threefold: natya, nritya and nritta, in order.

3181Of these, natya is thus:
The various states of people's nature in all their kinds,
joined with abhinaya of the body — that is natya.787

3182Thus [it is said]:
The nature of people, consisting of manifold states,
joined with abhinaya of the body, is called natya by the wise.

3183And further:
That which is in drama is by nature abhinaya of the meaning of sentences and the meaning of words;
of these the first, endowed with rasa and bhava, was set forth by Bharata;
and surely the lords of sages employed it in dramas and the like.788

3184Now, nritya:
That which is accepted by the custom of a country and rests on tala and the rest —
movement of the limbs with vilasa — is known as nritya.

3185Thus [it is said]:
That which is accepted by the custom of a country and rests on tala, mana and laya —
movement of the limbs with vilasa — the wise call nritya.

3186Vilasa is thus:
A particularity in actions — in looking at the beloved (nayaka) and the like —
accompanied by amorous movements, is called vilasa.

3187[It is told] of nritta:
The mark of what is called nritta is that it is devoid of all abhinaya;
it is known as mere movement of the limbs and the like.

3188Thus [it is said]:
Mere movement of the body, devoid of all abhinaya,
[performed] in the manner set forth for angika, the knowers of dance call nritta.

3189Natya, nritya and nritta — all three are of two kinds:
the distinction of marga and deshi — this is well known in the shastras.

3190Thus [it is said]:
These three are declared twofold — by the distinction of marga and deshi.

3191Of these, [it is told] of marga:
What was sought by Brahma and the others from Shambhu and employed by Bharata and the others —
song, instrumental music and dance — that is called marga.
(Margitam — that is, "sought.")

3192[It is told] of deshi:
The song, instrumental music and also dance that in various countries
supremely delight kings and others the wise call deshi.789

3193Twenty [kinds] of marga natya are defined by Kohala:
nataka, prakarana, bhana, prahasana and the rest.790

3194Some say marga natya is of ten kinds;
natika, prakaranika and the rest are [also] known.

3195Dattila and others name sixteen [kinds] of deshi natya:
sattaka, trotaka, goshthi, vrindaka and the rest.791

3196Such are the manifold parts of natya, pleasing to the mind;
here I have only pointed the way — [they] are well known in the shastras.

3197In nritya and nritta there are two [varieties]: tandava and lasya —
so say the knowers of dance; from them comes every happiness.

3198Thus [it is said]:
This pair is said to be twofold: tandava and lasya.
(The pair — that is, nritya and nritta.)

3199Tandava is a dance for the most part vigorous and the like;
for men and for women there are, respectively, tandava and lasya.

3200Thus [it is said]:
The performance, mostly vigorous, set forth by Tandu, they call tandava.
(Tandu is a particular [attendant] among the ganas of Shambhu.)792

3201In the Narada-samhita:
The dance of men is called tandava, the dance of women is called lasya.

3202Tandava is of two kinds: prerani tandava,
and also bahurupa tandava — this is commonly known.

3203Thus [it is said]:
Prerani and bahurupa — thus tandava is of two kinds.

3204Of these, prerani is thus:
Where there is abundance of bodily movement and also absence of abhinaya,
that is called prerani; among people its name is deshi.

3205Bahurupa is thus — in Damodara:
Where there is cutting and piercing, a manifold array of faces,
that is bahurupa tandava, vigorous, connected with speech.793

3206Prerani and bahurupa are described in detail elsewhere.
Lasya, which increases [the power of] Kandarpa, is well known in the shastras.

3207[It is told] of lasya:
The lasya dance is of two kinds: sphurita lasya,
and also yauvata lasya — these two are known everywhere.

3208Thus [it is said]:
Lasya, with tender movements of the body, increases [the power of] Makaradhvaja;
and it too is held to be twofold: sphurita and yauvata.794

3209[It is told] of sphurita lasya:
Where in the first [rasa], in abhinaya, with bhavas, rasas, embraces and kisses,
the nayika and the nayaka dance — that indeed is sphurita.
("In the first" — in the principal rasa; "with rasas" — with bhavas and movements that generate rasa; ashlesha — that is, embrace.)795

3210[It is told] of yauvata lasya:
Where actresses dance with sweet, well-knit pastimes,
resembling the science of enchantment — that lasya is held to be yauvata.

3211Now [it is told] of nritta:
Of nritta I shall give only the names: in it are three varieties —
vishama, vikata, laghu; the shastras set [them] out in detail.

3212Thus [it is said]:
Nritta too is declared threefold: vishama, vikata, laghu.
Vishama is said to be that in which there is whirling on a rope and the like;

3213vikata is held to be that in which dress, limbs and actions are grotesque;
laghu is known as that endowed with few karanas — anchita and the rest.
(Anchita and the rest are particular karanas; they will be described. The particular kinds of nritya named by Kohala — dombika, bhanika and the rest — have already been mentioned.)796

3214O Srinivasa! The ways of dance are manifold;
who has the power to tell of them completely?

3215In the Sri rasa-mandala Krishna, the crown of rasikas,
reveals a dance beyond the reach of Shiva and Brahma.

3216Who can keep composure at Krishna's wondrous dance?
Rai together with the sakhis floats in an ocean of happiness.

3217In dancing with one another great merriment grows;
a supreme wonder is that abhinaya of the body.

3218Now, anga abhinaya:
Abhinaya of the body is threefold: anga, upanga, and also
pratyanga; these three have many varieties.797

3219Thus [it is said]:
Here, according to our understanding, a description of the angas, upangas
and pratyangas is given, in agreement with Sharngadeva and others.798

3220The angas of abhinaya are the head, the shoulders, I say further,
the chest, the sides, the hands, the waist, the feet — so it is known.

3221Thus [it is said]:
The seven angas: head, shoulders, chest, sides, hands, waist, feet.

3222The pratyangas, know, are of nine beautiful kinds:
the neck, the arms, the shoulders, the wrists, the back, the belly,

3223the thighs, and also the shanks, the knees, the ornaments — these are the nine;
the abhinaya of the pratyangas is defined by the knowers of dance.799

3224Thus [it is said]:
The pratyangas are nine: neck, arms, shoulders, wrists,
back, belly, thighs, shanks, knees and ornaments.

3225The upangas are twelve; their abhinaya has its own kinds:
the crown, the gaze, the pupils, the brows, the face and the rest are known.800

3226Thus [it is said]:
The twelve upangas: the crown, the gaze, the pupils, the brows, the face,
the two nostrils, the breath and the chin, the tongue, the cheeks, the teeth, the lips;

3227and the color of the face Sharngadeva included among the upangas.801

3228Some say: the angas are six, the pratyangas ten,
and the abhinaya of the upangas is of twenty-three kinds.

3229All this is extensive; the chief in this are the angas;
something [of them] I shall make known, so as to attract all hearts.

3230Thus [it is said]:
Since among them the angas are chief, they are told of in brief.

3231Of them, first [it is told] of the head:
The actions of the head — dhuta, vidhuta, adhuta, and also
avadhuta and the rest — are of fourteen kinds.802

3232Thus [it is said]:
Dhuta, vidhuta, adhuta, avadhuta and kampita,
akampita and udvahita, parivahita, anchita,

3233nikunchita, paravritta, utkshipta and adhomukha,
and lolita — thus it should be known: the head is of fourteen kinds.
(Akampita means slightly trembling.)

3234Of them, dhuta:
A slow, slightly slanting shaking of the head is dhuta;
dhuta is prescribed for sorrow, wonder and the like.

3235Thus [it is said]:
The head slowly shaken sideways is called dhuta;
it occurs in refusal, in what is unwanted, in sorrow and in wonder.

3236Know the characteristics of vidhuta and the rest in the same way.
Likewise clear and well accepted is the abhinaya of the shoulders.

3237Now, the shoulders:
The shoulders are of five [kinds]: ekochcha, lagna-karna, and also
uchchhrita, srasta, lolita — such are the known characteristics.

3238Thus [it is said]:
Ekochcha, lagna-karna, uchchhrita, srasta and lolita —
so are named the five kinds of shoulders, whose characteristics are clear from the name itself.

3239The abhinaya ekochcha is in blows with the fist and the spear;
likewise in the shastras [are described] the characteristics of karna-lagna and the rest.

3240Thus [it is said]:
The shoulders are called ekochcha in blows with the fist and the spear;
in embracing and in cold the shoulders are karna-lagna, in the opinion of the virtuous;

3241uchchhrita in joy, pride and the like; srasta in grief, weariness, intoxication;
in fainting, and also in the dance of the vita, lolita should be done;
the knowers of dance name [it] in laughter and in playing the hudduka.803
(Vita-nartana means the dance of a paramour.)
Thus the shoulders are of five kinds.

3242Now, the chest:
The abhinaya of the chest is of five [kinds]: sama, abhugna, and also
nirbhugna, kampita, udvahita — so it is known.

3243Thus [it is said]:
The chest is sama, abhugna, nirbhugna, prakampita
and udvahita — of five kinds; their characteristics we set forth.

3244Of them, sama:
Know: the abhinaya sama is [when] the chest is in saushthava and the like;
the characteristics of abhugna and the rest the knowers of the shastras define.804

3245Thus [it is said]:
The chest established in saushthava, resting on the body in the chaturasra position,
remaining in its natural state, they call sama; sama is in the abhinaya of the natural state.
And so on.

3246Now, the sides:
The sides: vivartita, apasrita, prasarita,
nata, unnata — these five characteristics are known.

3247Thus [it is said]:
Vivartita, apasrita, prasarita, then nata
and unnata — so the wise have described the sides as of five kinds.
From the turning of the trika in turning round, there is vivartita.
And so on.
(Of the trika means of the back; "the trika is the lower part of the spine.")

3248Now, the hands:
The abhinaya of the hands is threefold: that called samyuta, and also
asamyuta and nritya-hasta — these three are known.

3249Thus [it is said]:
Asamyuta, samyuta and nritya-hastas — thus threefold
the hastakas are described by the knowers, by the distinction of ordinary and dance [gestures].805

3250The action of abhinaya with one hand is asamyuta;
the action that [is done] with both hands is samyuta.

3251[Gestures] that remain only in dance and express nothing,
with anga-hava, are called nritya-hasta.806

3252Thus [it is said]:
Those whose actions [are done] with one hand are asamyuta;
those whose action is with both hands are samyuta.

3253But those that remain only in dance and denote nothing,
accompanied by anga-hava, are held to be nritya-hastas.

3254The movement of the hands, the knowers of dance say, is threefold:
uttana, parshvaga, adhomukha — these three.

3255Thus [it is said]:
Uttana, parshvaga, and also adhomukha —
the movement of the hands of three kinds has been proclaimed by Bharata.807

3256Some say fifteen; this too I accept.
In order, according to the teaching, I shall make known the asamyuta.

3257The asamyuta is told of:
The asamyuta hastakas — pataka, and also
tripataka and the rest — are of twenty-four kinds.

3258Some say there are four more than these;
some say thirty; this is well accepted.

3259The asamyuta, by force of meaning, are accepted [also] as samyuta;
all this the learned define in detail.

3260Thus [it is said]:
Pataka, tripataka, [the gesture] named ardhachandra, kartarimukha,
arala-mushti, shikhara, kapittha, khatakamukha,

3261shukatunda, kangula, padmakosha, then pallava,
suchimukha, sarpashiras, chatura, mrigashirshaka,

3262hamsasya, hamsapaksha, bhramara, and also mukula,
urnanabha, samdamsha, tamrachuda, and one more — kavi:
these asamyuta hastas, it is said, are twenty-four.808

3263Upadhana, simhamukha, kadamba and nikunjaka —
these four besides, among the asamyuta, others have named.

3264By Damodara these asamyuta hastas are stated as thirty;
and the asamyuta, by force of meaning, are also samyuta.

3265What the characteristics of all these hastakas are,
and in what matters they are applied — this is set forth in the shastras.

3266The characteristics of the hastakas are very extensive;
here I show [only] the direction — how the abhinaya is.

3267Pataka is told of:
The thumb bent and resting at the base of the forefinger,
and all the other fingers straight — so pataka is known.

3268Thus [it is said]:
That whose thumb, being bent, rests at the base of the forefinger,
and whose [other] fingers are straight [and] joined, is called pataka.

3269Abhinaya with pataka is in touching and in many [other] cases;
the knowers of dance explain it in various ways.

3270Thus [it is said]:
It [is used] in touching, in peta, in [showing] flags, clapping and the like;
in [showing] flames its fingers, raised upward, are spread apart and moving;809

3271in [showing] streams they are lowered; in [showing] the wings of birds it is at the hips; in [showing] what is high it goes upward, but in pushkara and in seizing, downward;

3272in the abhinaya of tossing up the hand goes upward from the region of the hips.
("From the region of the hips" means from the place of the hips.)

3273In [expressing] facing [someone, the hand] comes from one's own side to the region of the face; trembling at the side in refusal; in dividing, apart at the sides.

3274And pataka [is used] slowly in rubbing, kneading, and also in cleaning;
in holding, pulling out and the like of large things — stones and so on —
these two [hands], turned toward each other, should be raised and lowered.
(Uchchhrita means raised upward.)

3275[The hand] with palm and fingers raised, moving downward, in [showing] the force of wind and waves;
in pointing to a lake and a pond, having crossed as a svastika, they part.
(Saras, palvala means a small pond.)

3276The two patakas, having taken the form of a svastika, should be separated
in cutting, concealing, [showing] a mirror, speaking and wiping.
(Pronchhana — in the [common] speech, ponchhana.)

3277Making the hands with palms downward and upward, slightly extended,
one should show the shore, a hole, a crocodile, a house, a cave.

3278Although the uses of the hands have been told without distinction, still [they] are to be applied only following the usage of people.

3279About this it is said:
Observing the practice of people and relying on natya,
one should apply the hastakas according to this or that movement;
in rubbing, cutting, [showing] a mirror, dividing and the like this is indeed clear.
Thus is pataka.

3280So the knowers of dance define tripataka and the rest;
the wonder that is in this — could anyone else grasp it?

3281Thus are the asamyuta hastas. Now [it is told] of the samyuta, [coming next] in order:

3282The samyuta hastakas are defined as thirteen:
anjali, kapota, karkata, svastika and the rest.

3283Thus [it is said]:
Anjali and kapota, karkata, and also svastika,
dola, pushpaputa, utsanga, khataka-vardhamanaka,

3284gajadanta and avahittha, nishadha, and also makara
and vardhamana — these samyuta hastas are thirteen.810

3285Here, anjali:
Two patakas joined with the palms of both hands are anjali;
anjali is used in obeisance to the gods and the like.

3286Thus [it is said]:
If two patakas are joined at the palms, then it is anjali;
in obeisance to the gods it is said to be [held] above the head;

3287but in obeisance to the gurus it should be at the face;
and in obeisance to brahmanas, the virtuous hold, at the heart;

3288in others there is no rule, know this; [it] may be done in the three [ways] as one wishes. Thus is anjali.

3289The characteristics of kapota and the other samyuta [hastakas] are many;
the knowers of dance expound [them] in various ways.

3290Now, the nritya-hastas:
The nritya-hastas are suited only to dance;
they are of thirty kinds; some say thirty-two.

3291Chaturasra, udvritta and the rest — thirty kinds;
the characteristics and so on of them all are well set forth in the shastras.

3292Thus [it is said]:
Two chaturasras, then two udvrittas, the hands named tenamukha, and so on.811

3293The hastakas are endless; the learned [only] pointed out the direction,
and the other hastakas that [there are] they expounded by kinds.

3294Thus [it is said]:
These hastakas have been stated by me only to point out the direction;
because of the endlessness of what is portrayed, there are endless other [positions of the] hands.
Thus are the hands.

3295Now [it is told] of the hips:
The abhinaya of the hips is of five [kinds]: kampita, udvahita,
chhinna, vivrita, rechita — [such are] the known characteristics.

3296Thus [it is said]:
Kampita, udvahita, chhinna, vivrita, and also rechita —
so the hips are said to be of five kinds.

3297Now, the feet:
The feet: sama, anchita, kunchita, suchi and the rest —
thirteen kinds the knowers of dance define.

3298Thus [it is said]:
Sama, anchita, kunchita and suchi-agratala-sanchara,
mardita and udghatita, and also agraga, parshvaga and parshniga,812

3299tadita, udghattita, uchchhedha, udghatita — so in order;
the feet are said by the knowers of dance to be of thirteen kinds.813

3300When both feet stand naturally, [the foot] is called sama.
Thus are the seven angas.

3301What the abhinaya of the pratyangas and upangas is like —
this the knowers of dance have set forth in detail.

3302And whatever other acts of natya they introduced in this [teaching] —
all of that I cannot set forth in detail.

3303O Srinivasa! In the rasa the son of the king of Vraja
reveals what is hard to know [even] for Brahma and the others.

3304There is no comparison for [His] abhinaya of the body;
[He] reveals various bhavas in endless poses.

3305Sri Radhika and all Radhika's sakhis
reveal [such] poses — who could tell of [them], and how much?

3306The supreme, wondrous beauty cannot be told;
amid the sakhis Rai and Kanu sport.

3307What can be said of the captivating sweetness of the two of Them!
The best of the wise describe [it] in various ways.

3308Thus [it is said] in a song — of Sri Krishna, in a suitable raga:814
Shyama-raya, who delights in the rasa —
at [His] poses the world swoons.

3309Crushed collyrium, a dense mass of clouds —
these the luster of [His] most tender body surpasses.

3310On [His] head shines the eyed peacock feather;
[it] enchants the minds of the young women.

3311A wondrous tilaka on [His] lovely forehead;
whom do the curling locks not bewitch?

3312The two brows are Kama's bow;
in the corners of the eyes, arrows are aimed.

3313Restless earrings at the ears;
a pearl swings at the nostril.

3314The moon of [His] face, in all four directions,
rains nectar with a mere trace of a smile.

3315The sweetness of [His] broad chest
steals the wealth of composure.

3316On [His] neck the forest garland sports;
seeing [it], can a frail woman hold her heart?

3317The curve of [His] arms steals life;
with [His] slender waist [He] maddens the world.

3318[His] garments and ornaments are finely arrayed;
[His] thighs put to shame an upturned plantain trunk.815

3319Ankle bells ring on [His] reddish feet;
Narahari offers himself for Him.

3320[A song] in a suitable raga. Now, of Sri Radhika:
Rai, who delights in the rasa, in the rasa
sports amid the sakhis at Shyama's left side.

3321Ah, I die! What radiance of beauty!
It lights up the world, surpassing the whole array of comparisons.

3322With [Her] face [She] destroys the moon's conceit;
with [Her] sweetest smile [She] steals the pride of nectar.

3323[Her] two brows are a row of bees;
in the corners of [Her] lotus eyes — play of many kinds.

3324In [Her] nose a lovely pendant is set;
how fresh the dot of sindura in the middle of the forehead!

3325In [Her] ears, charming earrings;
the beauty of [Her] cheeks puts a golden mirror to shame.

3326On [Her] hands bracelets and bangles shine;
[Her] breasts, covered with a bodice, enchant Kanu's mind.

3327[Her] slender waist is girdled with kinkini bells;
the wondrous garment She wears clings to [Her] body.

3328Graceful are [Her] hips and thighs;
did the one who fashioned [them] keep even a trace of composure?

3329Jeweled ankle bells on [Her] feet;
Narahari offers himself for the rays of [Her] lovely nails.

3330Rai and Kanu with the sakhis, in various ways,
fulfil the desire of Sri Vrinda-devi.

3331What joy arises in the Sri rasa-mandala!
The mridanga and many [other] instruments sound in one accord.

3332Shyama-raya, the crest-jewel of rasikas, dances;
with what longing the poet sings the sweetness of that dance!

3333Thus [it is said] in a song (raga Kedara):
The Nagara of Vraja dances, ocean of rasa, abode of happiness.
The anklets on [His] feet jingle; in various gaits [He] keeps the tala,
stealing the [whole] weight of composure; [His] abundant poses are incomparable. (Refrain.)

3334The host of fair maidens is seized with delight; hastakas of many kinds,
new abhinaya of the bowed head — the peacock feather tilted to the left.
Lovely are [His] face and lips — [they] drive away the conceit of the moon and the dawn;
[His] kunda-jasmine teeth flash; [His] sweet smile conquers Kama.

3335How many lovely pathas [He] calls out: "Dha dha dhiki dhiki taka tata,
thai thai thai thai di drimiki, drimikata didi drama!
Tatta taka thok thoga, thavi kukudha dhilanga,
dhikata dhidhi kata, dhidhi dhilli lili" — how charming!816

3336Delightful is the sound of the ornaments at [His] waist; a flower garland hangs on [His] chest;
the rows of [His] locks sway — fine, charming on [His] forehead.
The jewels of the earrings flash in [His] ears; surpassing restless young khanjana birds
is the glance of [His] lotus eyes; Ghanashyama offers himself [for this].817

3337Again, raga Kedara:
Shyama, full of rasa, shines amid the rasa-mandala in beautiful poses;
in lovely attire, playful, supremely skilled in ever new music.

3338Relishfully [He] displays jatis, shrutis, svaras, gramas, murchhanas, tanas;818
"Thodita kata thaita thai thai," [He] says, smiling ever so gently.

3339The lovely moon of [His] face flashes, breaking the weight of Madana's pride;
the glance of [His] restless lotus eyes delights the hearts of the young women.

3340On [His] feet shine the anklets that sound "jhana nana nana";
Narahari offers himself for the sweet dance; the mridanga sounds: "drimi drimi."

3341Again, raga Bhupali:
Shyama-raya the rasika dances;
seeing [Him], whose heart does not find solace?

3342In what sweet manner [He] smiles gently!
[He] destroys the composure and dharma of the young women.819

3343The earrings swing at the base of [His] ears;
whom does the radiance of [His] cheeks not bewitch?

3344How much abhinaya [He] performs,
by which Madana is defeated!

3345From the corners of [His] restless long eyes
what rasa [He] pours out — who knows?

3346With [His] lotus feet [He] keeps the tala;
the sound of the ankle bells steals life.

3347"Ta thai ta thai thai thaiya" —
with what grace [He] says it, lingering, lingering!

3348Drimi drimi sounds the madal;
Narahari offers up [his] life [for this].

3349O Srinivasa, Rai's dance is wondrous;
the poets describe [something of it] but find no end [to it].

3350Thus [it is said] in a song (raga Kedara):
Radha dances, shattering the weight of composure, with the gait of an elephant.
Auspicious, stainless, soft is the bank of the Kalindi;
blessed, blessed, blessed are the pure, splendid bank [and] night, full of rasa! (Refrain.)

3351Ever so softly sounds the mridanga: "Dhigi dhigi dhigi taga dhilanga,
dha drinda drinda jhendrang drimi, drimi drimi drimi dramini."
Jhunu nunu — the sound of the ankle bells on [Her] feet; the kinkini bells at [Her] waist — jhini nini nini;
the bangles on [Her] hands tinkle: jhanana, jhanana — [She is] exceedingly charming.

3352The lotus of [Her] face in bloom, [Her] garment, the rows of teeth, the graceful laughter;820
"Taka thai thai, thai taka," [She] utters, the abode of happiness.
Most lovely is the host of jeweled ornaments; [She] sways [Her] neck in dense delight;
restless are the corners of [Her] eyes [and Her] brows; the host of [Her] locks adorns [Her].

3353Stealing the pride of gold, with a body of supreme sweetness,
veiled by the fluttering end of [Her] garment, the Incomparable One shines.
[She] makes hastakas of many kinds; beauty, a mass of rasa, pours [from Her];
Narahari, beholding, offers himself again and again [for Her]; the celestial women are put to shame.

3354Again, raga Karnata:
Radha, who delights in the rasa, dances;
the mridanga sounds: "dhik dhik dha dha."

3355The rays of [Her] body flash, stealing the mind;
the smile of [Her] moon-face — as if nectar were pouring.

3356[She] calls out: "Thai thai dhiki taka dhenna,
ai ati ai ati oia tenna."

3357The movement of [Her] lotus eyes crushes the khanjana birds;
[Her] hands, performing abhinaya, are adorned with bracelets.

3358[Her] slender waist is girdled with jingling kinkini bells;
the garment She wears is light [and] clings to [Her] body.

3359Jhanana — the jeweled ankle bells flash on [Her] feet;
Narahari offers himself for the grace with which [She] steps.

3360Again, raga Kamoda:
Rai dances, the jewel among women;
on [Her] feet the ankle bells ring, at [Her] waist the kinkini.

3361[Her] braid, surpassing a serpent, swings on [Her] back;
what a curve of the neck — in waves of rasa!

3362What sweet abhinaya [She] performs!
Saying "tathaia tathaia thaiya," [She] keeps the tala.

3363Destroying with [Her] face the moon's conceit,
with [Her] smile [She] rains nectar — heaps upon heaps!

3364Abhinaya of the eyes — in how many ways!
[She] intoxicates King Madana, the Moon of Vraja.

3365What comparison can Narahari give?
The beauty of [Her] body lights up the world.

3366O Srinivasa, with what delight Rai and Kanu
perform a wondrous dance together with Lalita and the others!

3367Thus [it is said] in a song (raga Kedara):
Today the play of the rasa is supreme; Shyama shines, full of the highest rasa;
Radhika's lotus hand is with the Upholder of the mountain, who delights [all] with [His] steps.821
With smiling face [He] calls out lovely pathas: "Thai tathai thai tathai tatatho, didi digan" —
the abhinaya of [His] hands breaks the weight of Madana's pride.

3368The jewel of women sees the face of her beloved, her very life, and deep joy grows in [her] heart;
[her] whole body thrills abundantly, [her] soles keep the tala in restless movement.
It sounds: "Drimi drimiki drimidha, thai tathai tata thai tathai tha,
thung nung nung"; from the corners of [her] restless eyes a wealth of rasa rains down.

3369Beholding the beauty of the Couple, delighted, offering themselves for the incomparable cloud and lightning, Lalita and her friends, absorbed in the dance, gently, gently sway their necks in lovely poses. In sweet voices, in many ways, [they] utter: "Thai tathai thai drimiki drimi tatho, dig dig dig dig thai tathai" — with surpassing skill, in fine music.

3370Beautifully attired, Vishakhika dances on [her] side, again and again crying: "Tadhik dhigiti, dhigiti dhigi dhigi dhik dhaikata, dha dhi ni ni ni nini dhinnina." "Drimiki drimi drimi" — the sound of the mardala steals composure; Ghanashyama says unceasingly: "Tiai aiti aia, aiati aia tinnina."

3371Again, raga Kedara:
What a fresh full-moon night it is today!
The bank of the Yamuna flashes in the rasa; the moon lights up the quarters.

3372Rai and Kanu — in what a sweet manner the two of Them dance, leaning against each other, resting [Their] arms on [each other's] shoulders!

3373Every moment, what delight in [Their] hearts! Both play the flute, bringing [Their] faces together — what comparison could be given for that?

3374Eyes in lovely eyes,
lips touch lips, [tasting] rasa; in rapture the heart rejoices.

3375With both hands, the left and the right,
They display so many kinds of abhinaya, stealing Madana's composure.

3376"Ta ta tathai tathai," They say;
ceaseless is that sound — what a stream of nectar flows from the moon of [Their] faces!

3377Drimi drimiki — the mridanga sounds;
on the ground the feet keep the tala — how finely the new ankle bells adorn [them]!

3378Lalita and the others, seeing that beauty,
sing in various ways with dancing gestures — [a beauty] that entices Narahari's mind.

3379O Srinivasa, the pastimes of the rasa dance the poets
describe in detail — in them is endless bliss.

3380Hearing all this destroys many misfortunes;
the lotus feet of Radha and Krishna are attained without effort.

3381Krishna, the Enjoyer of the Sri rasa dance, the Enchanter of the worlds,
sports in the water of the Yamuna for a long while.

3382Who can describe the merriment in that?
In this kunja dwelling [They] array Themselves in wondrous attire.

3383The Two lie down here in great joy;
at the end of night the sakhis wake [Them].

3384The Two, with the sakhis, go each to Their own home;
in separation from each other, the Two cannot keep hold of life.

3385The sakhis console the Two in many ways;
the Two, lying down each in Their own home, meet in dreams.

3386Thus [it is said] in a song:
Rai and Shyama-raya with the sakhis —
abundant play in the rasa dance, jubilation in the heart.

3387To sport in the water,
entering the waters of the Yamuna, [They] make so many graceful movements.

3388[They] shower water on each other;
the garments get wet, clinging to the bodies, full of beauty.

3389Abashed, the lovely girl, glancing toward Shyama,
hides in the deep water, in a forest of lotuses.

3390That Dark One, beside Himself with prema,
kisses a lotus, mistaking [it] for Rai's face.

3391Lalita and the other sakhis all around,
seeing Shyama's antics, laugh ever so softly.

3392Rai, receiving a sign from the sakhis,
stands leaning Her body against Shyama's body.

3393Moment by moment the merriment grows;
having sported in the water, [They] come up onto the bank of the Yamuna.

3394Intoxicated by Madana, They drink honey;
in the joy of the battle of love the heart overflows.

3395At the end of night, from the nikunja,
[They] go with wary steps by unseen paths.

3396The Two, having gone each to Their own home,
lie down, distraught with the pain of separation.

3397In dreams [They] meet, with joy in the heart;
Narahari offers himself up for this love of the Two.

3398Coming again, [They] sport in this kunja dwelling;
the poets describe this in order, in various ways.

3399Thus [it is said] in the Govinda-lilamrita, in the first canto, the fourth verse:822
He who at the end of night goes from the kunja into the cowherd village, in the morning and in the evening performs the pastimes of milking, eating and the like,
in the sangava, grazing the cows, sports with His friends,
at midday and then at night verily enjoys with Radha in the forest, in the afternoon
goes to the village, and at pradosha delights His dear ones — may that Krishna protect us.

3400Thus [it is said] in a song:
At the end of night, lying in a new kunja,
the ornaments of Vraja, Shyama and Gori, in fresh love,
waking playfully, in fear of the stern elders,
go very swiftly and lie down again at home.

3401In the morning, busy with bathing and so on, the lovely girl,
having gone to Yashomati's house, cooks together with the sakhis.
Kanu milks the cows, bathes happily,
and, having eaten with His companions, [enjoys] the many delights of rest.

3402In the forenoon [He] goes to the forest with the cows;
having played, [He] nimbly hastens to the bank of the kunda.
Enduring separation from the beloved, the lovely girl again
restlessly watches the path of the messenger She Herself has sent.

3403At midday the beautiful girl with the sakhis near Her own kunda
rejoices, having met the beloved:
stealing the flute, drinking honey, bathing, worship of the Sun,
and so many other varied pastimes.

3404Gori goes home and in the afternoon, having dressed,
with the sakhis keeps gazing at the beloved's path.
Shyama goes home with the cows and His friends;
seeing that face, the people of Vraja are filled with great happiness.

3405In the evening the mother fondles [Him];
milking the cows and so on — much merriment.
The various foods sent by Rai
[He] happily eats together with dear Subala and the others.823

3406At the time of pradosha the Nagara of Vraja, having dressed
and listened to the singing of the skilled, goes to the kunja.
Rai, the jewel of women, adorned, with unseen steps
[goes] with the sakhis, full of joy at meeting Shyama.

3407In the sweet night, engaged in new dance and song —
the pastimes of the rasa dance, unequalled in the world;
in the kunja house, the love-play and quarrels of the Two;
the sakhis [and] Ghanashyama happily serve [Them] at rest.

3408O Srinivasa, here, on this bank of the Yamuna,
Krishna swings with His beloved on a wondrous swing.

3409Thus [it is said] in a song (raga Mallara):
Today the King of nagaras swings
in the midst of a most lovely nikunja.

3410Ropes freshly made of jewels;
on them [He] shines, lost in delight.

3411On the left side the beautiful girl shines,
charming the mind of Shyamasundara.

3412The beauty of the Two is an incomparable radiance:
lightning and the massed clouds are left far [behind].

3413On the bodies are ornaments of gold and jewels,
and on them most wondrous garments.

3414On the neck a lovely necklace sways;
the play of the eyes — what can compare with it?

3415On the moons of the faces, a most sweet smile;
ceaselessly a flood of nectar pours.

3416The Two, placing lips to lips,
remain with body blended with body.

3417Lalita and the other sakhis all around,
seeing this play, float in such bliss!

3418Laughing, they swing [the swing] gently, gently;
together they sing songs in fine measure.

3419Some play the mridanga and other [instruments];
some wave a lovely chamara whisk.

3420Endless are the signs of the rainy season;
a gentle breeze blows over the lovely land.

3421All around, trees and creepers, delightful [to see];
many flowers in abundant bloom.

3422Bees wander, their humming everywhere;
peacocks, cuckoos, many birds.

3423Loud and thick is the voice of the frogs;
the rain-clouds of rasa hang low, pouring down.

3424Whatever comparison one tells is too little;
Ghanashyama is lost in this merriment.

3425Look, Srinivasa, [here is] the place of the Holi play;824
here — what wondrous pastimes of Rai and Kanu!

3426In a song (raga Vasanta):
Today in supreme delight and joy Shyama, the King of connoisseurs of rasa,
having dressed, sports in the midst of a new kunja house.

3427Radha, moon-faced, adorned — no comparison is enough;
beside Her Beloved, in graceful poses, She shines, overwhelmed with rasa.825

3428The Two throw phagu on each other's bodies — [the bodies] became crimson;
musk, sandal, fragrant pollen, kunkuma They apply again.

3429The companions, seeing the manifold beauty of the Two,
play so many instruments and sing of [Their] deeds, mad with joy.

3430The restless Enchanter of the mind again and again shoots [a jet] from the pichkari;
body and garment are soaked — struck [by the jet], the tender [girl] is startled.826

3431Lalita pours water with ground collyrium on the Nagara's head;
shouting "Ho, ho, ho, hori!" she claps her hands.

3432The best of dancers, skilled in playful quarrels, seizes one and draws her near —
He kisses [her] face; on another's lotus breast He places His hand.

3433Another He embraces again and again, speaking most sweet words;
He rains the arrows of His glances — at the touch the body thrills.

3434Who could reach the end of the joy of such phagu play?
The king of seasons, the spring, deems [it] the fruit of its great merit.

3435Auspiciously — "Jaya, jaya!" — the cuckoos call ceaselessly.
What can Ghanashyama say? I offer myself up for this boundless merriment!

3436O Srinivasa, here [there was] a great merriment:
by the wish of the sakhis Rai became the Kunja-devi.827

3437Thus [it is said] in a song (in any raga):
The beautiful girl, having taken counsel with the sakhis,
merrily sets out to meet Shyama.
Entering the nikunja, She sits alone, happily,
covering Her body with a lovely cloth.

3438The best of nagaras, under a tree, restless,
gazes at Rai's path under the weight of prema.
Looking at that lovely girl in the kunja, He rushes [there],
goes up and quietly asks Vrinda-devi:

3439"Tell me, tell me: who, alone in the new nikunja,
sits in such unprecedented attire?
Such beauty I have never seen on earth —
how could [even] Uma's form compare [with her]?"

3440Hearing this, Vrinda says to the son of the king of Vraja:
"This is the goddess of this nikunja.
All my power — know this, You —
comes from serving her feet."

3441Hearing these words, the one versed in rasa, intent on going,
with the greatest reverence, in hope of seeing [Her],
restless of heart, entering the lovely kunja,
stands beside that new goddess.

3442Joining both hands, He says: "Today all
[my] desires will be fulfilled through serving you.
Do not deceive [me], be merciful — [I] shall be happy;
I humbly make my plea — listen, O goddess!

3443"My beloved, dear as life, the darling of my heart,
the daughter of Vrishabhanu, the jewel of women —
not seeing her, my life cannot bear;
a moment I count as so many hundreds of yugas.

3444"She is of a noble family, always very gentle;
her heart trembles in fear of the elders.
Therefore, O bestower of good, do this,
so that no one can say anything to her."

3445Having said this, Kanu bows down,
touching [Her] feet, offering a handful of flowers.
Seeing that, Lalita and the others, staying hidden,
laugh, their hearts thrilling exceedingly.

3446Vrinda-devi says: "What are You doing, Dark One?
What fruit will You gain from such worship?
With each limb [of Yours] worship each limb [of hers] —
only then will this goddess be pleased."

3447Hearing this, the Moon-faced One, keeping Her face under the veil,
smiles softly, floating in bliss.
She who with the corner of Her eye restrains Vrinda
[Herself] again shows a slight smile.

3448Maddened by the intoxication of Madana, the Nagara,
seeing [this], laughs, floating in the waters of bliss:
"Come, come, my goddess, dear as life!" —
saying this, He lifts [Her] and takes [Her] onto His lap.

3449Lalita, leaving [her hiding place] among the creepers, [comes] near
and says, "How much shall I admonish [You]?
Calling [her] Kunja-devi, You are not afraid at all —
[yet] You are a rake, eager for viparita-rati.828

3450Do You see no sin in this?" Hearing, [He] answers,
"The sin will go, receiving your touch."
Hearing this, the sakhis together with Narahari
laugh, covering their mouths with the ends of their cloth.

3451O Srinivasa! One day here
Sri Krishna became greatly agitated without Rai.

3452Hearing from the mouth of a messenger that Radhika was coming,
the son of the king of Vraja became mad with great joy.

3453He fixed His eyes and mind on the path by which Radhika was coming,
and became so bewildered that He did not know Himself.

3454And here Radha, by the wish of [Her] dear sakhis,
goes to Krishna as if a messenger of Chandravali.

3455Thus [it is said] in a song (in any raga):
Nectar-faced Radha, keeping the happy sakhis
at some distance, in great merriment,
[His] beloved, dear as life, goes alone to [Him],
unrecognized — a messenger of Chandravali.829

3456In the nikunja the nagara, all atremble, in the hope
of seeing Rai, is beside Himself.
How many desires He cherishes in His mind,
and again and again He looks toward the path of His beloved.

3457And there the bees in multitudes hover and play,
humming as if on some pretext.
"Chandravali's messenger — why does she wander in the forest?" —
not understanding, the Dark One starts on hearing [of her].

3458At that very moment that messenger quickly
came up to [Him], looking at Him.
[His] face became gloomy and darkened;
knowing [He was] in a fix, [He was] troubled in mind.

3459Steadying Himself again, displaying cunning,
[He] says affectionately to the messenger,
"Go, [I am] right behind you, I will follow quickly."
The messenger says, "I cannot go [without You].

3460Without You Chandravali does not live —
why do You delay? Go and see her state!
Get up, get up, there can be no more delay!" —
so saying, she rushes [to Him] and seizes [His] feet.

3461At the touch — and the messenger's touch is the supreme [bliss] —
in how many ways He seems to hold on to His composure!
Receiving the sweet touch of the messenger, the moon Shyama
became helpless, as if bitten by a snake.

3462With restless eyes He looks at Vrinda
and says, "Tell Me, tell Me, what has happened to Me?"
Vrinda says, "Why worry? It will be well —
embrace the messenger just once."

3463Hearing, the jewel of the clever unrestrainedly
embraces the messenger and floats in bliss.
All the sakhis, watching this from afar,
look at Vrinda and smile slightly.

3464Lalita, [coming out] from among the lovely mallika jasmine creepers,
in anger, frowning, says,
"Go, go there — there is no point in [Your] staying here;
Your incomparable ways I cannot bear.

3465However much You [pretend], O rake —
let all those words stay aside:
what there is between You and Chandravali,
that I have learned through the messenger.

3466Ah, how wonderful is Your love of this kind:
the thrill of ecstasy is never seen on [Your] body [with us].
Why be shy before all of us?
Drink the nectar of Chandravali to Your heart's content!"

3467Hearing, Kanu says, "This moon-like face,
surpassing Chandravali, is a heap of nectar.
I have received permission — now I shall drink," —
so saying, smiling, He kisses [Her] face.830

3468Taking [Her] by the chin with His sprout-like hand,
He jests in the rapture of rasa;
seating [Her] on His thighs, adorning [Her] beautifully,
He sports [with Her] on a new couch.

3469Knowing the time is right, two dear sakhis
carefully relieve [Their] fatigue.
Receiving a sign, Narahari joyfully
fans [Them] with a chamara, beholding Their beauty.

3470O Srinivasa, and how [They] sport in this rasa-kunja —
who can tell?

3471The sakhi unfolds the supremely wonderful lila,
and with joy of heart the sakhi relishes it.

3472Without a sakhi joy never arises;
the greatness of the sakhi is known everywhere.

3473Thus [it is said] in the Ujjvala-nilamani, in [the section on] the kinds of sakhis, the first verse: The sakhi is she who fully unfolds the pastimes of prema, and [she is also] a casket for the jewel of trust; therefore [she] is examined here in detail.

3474O Srinivasa, Krishna is the embodiment of rasa;
what power have I to tell which lilas [He performed] in which places?

3475In all the varieties of nayaka He sports;
the crown of nayakas is the son of the king of Vraja.

3476Thus [it is said] in the Bhakti-rasamrita-sindhu:
The crest-jewel of nayakas is Krishna, the Supreme Lord Himself.

3477By the distinction of abodes the kinds of nayaka are ninety-six, 96;
in Vraja Krishna is purnatama, [His] bhava is upapati.831

3478With thousands upon thousands of yutheshvaris
He playfully displays the acts of all [kinds of] nayaka.832

3479Among the yuthas the most excellent are Chandravali and Sri Radhika;
everywhere it is known that of them Radhika is the higher.

3480Thus [it is said] in the Ujjvala-nilamani:
But even among them, in every way the most excellent are the two — Radha and Chandravali,
whose yuthas [number] millions of doe-eyed ones.

3481The rasa was crowded with hundreds of millions of young maidens
on that bank of the Yamuna — such is the tradition of the agamas.

3482But even of these two Radhika is higher in every way:
She is the embodiment of mahabhava; She far surpasses [all] in qualities.

3483What Krishna's pastimes with Sri Radhika are like —
who has the power to describe that in detail?

3484Here Krishna sports in the greatest merriment,
displaying the acts of a dhirodatta nayaka.

3485The dhirodatta is highly skilled in every respect,
supremely grave, [his] ways pure — humility and the rest.

3486Thus [it is said] in the Bhakti-rasamrita-sindhu:
Grave, humble, forbearing, compassionate, firm in his vows,
not boastful, with hidden pride, magnanimous — [such is] the dhirodatta.
This one is like Raghunatha.833

3487Krishna, the charming dhiralalita nayaka,
sports unceasingly in this kunja temple.

3488Clever, carefree, very fond of jesting,
subject to His beloved, [His] ways are supreme bliss.

3489There:
Clever, in fresh youth, a master of jests,
carefree — [such is] the dhiralalita; he is mostly subject to his beloved.
This one is like Kandarpa.

3490The dhirashanta nayaka is Sri, the son of the king of Vraja,
a knower of the shastras, master of His senses, supremely righteous.

3491He displays humility and other virtues at His beloved's side;
in this kunja house there are wonderfully marvellous pastimes.

3492There:
Even-tempered, enduring hardship, discerning,
endowed with humility and other virtues — [such a one] is called dhirashanta.
This one is like Yudhishthira.

3493Whatever the virtues and acts of a dhiroddhata nayaka are,
Krishna displays [them] here so that His beloved rejoices.

3494Self-praise and the rest in Him are the greatest wonder;
the merriment that [was] in this kunja cannot be described in full.

3495There:
Jealous, proud, wily, wrathful, fickle
and boastful — [such a one] the wise have called dhiroddhata.
This one is like Bhimasena.

3496O Srinivasa, Krishna, the embodiment of rasa,
revealed the ways of an anukula nayaka.

3497There is no equal to the anukula nayaka:
anukula is attachment to one nayika.

3498The anukula nayaka is Sri, the prince of Vraja;
here are [His] wonderful pastimes with Rai alone.

3499Thus [it is said] in the Ujjvala-nilamani:
He who, through excessive attachment to [one] woman, has given up longing for other beauties,
like Rama toward Sita — he is called anukula.

3500Toward Radha alone is Krishna's famed devotion (anukulata):
at the sight of Her He never recalls association with others.

3501How Krishna is subject to Radha's prema, what the love of the two of Them is —
that way the poets describe in various manners.

3502Thus [it is said] in the Gaura-charitra-chintamani — Sri Yamuna speaks to Ganga — in a song (raga Pauravi):834
O you, dear [to me] as life, friend full of joy!
I am sold to your virtues.
Now I shall tell — listen: [of her]
with whom Shyamasundara's love is greater.

3503Chandravali in Vraja is a renowned beauty;
before [her] wondrous beauty Rama is ashamed;
a young beauty full of rasa —
in virtues and character she has no equal.

3504In a fine new nikunja temple
she sports merrily with Shyama every day;
Shyama, full of rasa, is likewise enraptured —
who can grasp the way of [His] subjection to her prema?

3505When [He] floats in the ocean of supreme bliss,
touching that jewel of a beauty,
immersed in drinking the nectar of [her] moon-face —
then nothing [else] comes to the nagara's mind.

3506If at that time the fragrance of Radha's body,
reaching [Him], touches [His] nostrils ever so slightly —
at once, leaving her, the restless
Dark One runs as if gone mad.

3507What more shall I say? Know in your heart
with whom Kanu's love is greater.
Narahari offers himself for such prema —
who can find the bottom in counting [Her] virtues?

3508Again there (raga Kamoda):
What shall I say, O [friend]: incomparable in the world
is the love of Radha and Madhava.
The life is one, but the bodies separate: who
fashioned [Them so], with what joy?

3509If you say, "Since the two are one, why then
did the colour of the two become different?" —
of that I shall tell you a little;
listen to it with care.

3510There are many colours; among them is shyama,
[but] in the gaura colour there is greater beauty.
Showing its utmost to the world,
[it] shines, alluring the eyes of the people of the world.835

3511And I say more: O [friend], the restless Dark One,
when He sees playful Radha,
eagerly longing, spreads out both arms
and yearns to take [Her] in His embrace.

3512If at that time people of the rivals' party
suddenly see this nearby,
some, deceived by the semblance of a cloud with lightning,
cannot make out this great play.836

3513And I say more: that skilful poet, the Creator,
to give great joy to many people,
gazing on the loveliness of shyama and gaura,
[resolved,] "I shall compose comparisons in many ways."

3514That is why [They are] so [different] — [yet] not different at all:
Shyama's body is fashioned of Rai's prema.
The bodies of Radha and Kanu are full of prema —
the love of these bodies is known in the world.

3515The ways of these two — what will others know?
Only the rasikas know.
Whoever is deprived of this rasa,
Narahari counts him equal to a beast.

3516O Srinivasa, one day here
a meeting with Chandravali was arranged.

3517Krishna became eager to meet her;
she set out for the tryst with her own sakhis.

3518At that time, hearing that Radhika was going to the nikunja,
the son of the king of Vraja sets out from here.

3519Coming near Radhika, [He] lost His composure
and forgot everything — the meeting with Chandravali and the rest.

3520What pastimes there were in this kunja with Rai —
that I do not know how to tell, O Srinivasa.

3521Krishna is the dakshina-nayaka, His actions full of rasa;
one who is the same toward all nayikas is called dakshina.837

3522How Krishnachandra sports here with His beloveds —
who could tell it?

3523There:
One who, even with his heart given to another, does not abandon respect, fear, love and courtesy toward his former beloved —
he should be known as dakshina.838

3524Or:
Also one who is the same toward many nayikas is called dakshina.

3525The way that belongs to the nayaka who is dakshina and anukula
Krishna, the embodiment of rasa, displayed in the rasa [dance].

3526Thus [it is said] in the Chaitanya-charitamrita, in the Madhya-khanda, in the eighth chapter:
"The sacred rasa pastimes with a hundred crores of gopis;
among them, in one form He remains at Radha's side.839

3527Seeing ordinary love — equality everywhere —
Radha's crooked love turned into contrariness.

3528Angered, She left the rasa [dance] in pique and went away;
not seeing Her, Hari was distraught.

3529Krishna's whole desire, His wish, is the rasa-lila;
in the desire for the rasa-lila Radhika is the [binding] chain.

3530Without Her the rasa-lila does not please [His] heart;
leaving the circle, He went to search for Radha.

3531Wandering here and there and finding Radha nowhere,
He grieves, wearied by the arrows of Kama.

3532With a hundred crores of gopis [His] desire is not quenched —
from this I infer the virtues of Sri Radhika."

3533Here Krishna displays [the nature] of the shatha-nayaka:
to the face — pleasing; behind the back He acts unpleasingly.

3534Thus [it is said] in the Ujjvala-nilamani:
One who speaks pleasingly to her face, but elsewhere does much that is unpleasing
and [commits] a hidden offense — him the wise call shatha.

3535Here Krishna displays the actions of the dhrishta-nayaka
before the nayika, rejoicing.

3536Even with the marks of enjoyment with another nayika He is fearless,
exceedingly skilled in the use of false words.

3537There:
One who is fearless though the marks of enjoyment with another young [woman] are plain on him,
and skilled in false speech — he indeed is called dhrishta.

3538Here Krishna, with Radha, the beloved dear [to Him] as life,
[enjoys] pastimes in which He is beside Himself — who can describe them?

3539Radha, who is in the middle stage [of youth], is a mine of jewel-like virtues;
She is known as the crown of all nayikas.

3540As in Krishna the states of all nayakas are possible,
so in Sri Radhika are the states of all nayikas.

3541There:
As all the states of the nayaka without exception [belong] to Madhava,
so the states of the nayika, it is held, [belong] for the most part to Radha.

3542By distinction of place svakiya and parakiya are determined;
the varieties of nayika are three hundred and sixty.840

3543In Vraja Radha is the parakiya, the highest nayika;
in the varieties — mugdha and the rest — She sports without limit.841

3544O Srinivasa, in this nikunja house
Krishna sports with the mugdha-nayika.

3545The mugdha is under the sway of the sakhi, her youth fresh;
in the skill of the new arts of love she is little practised.

3546In mana she is gentle, incapable [of it];
having united her with Krishna, the sakhi attains great happiness.

3547There:
The mugdha has new youth and [new] desire, is contrary in union, under the sway of the sakhi,
exceedingly bashful in love's acts, [yet making] charming hidden efforts;

3548when the beloved has offended, her gaze is choked with tears; she is unable to speak either pleasing or unpleasing words, and in mana she always turns away.

3549She who turns away in mana is thus:
gentle, and also incapable [of mana] — so she who turns away in mana is of two kinds.842

3550Look at this nikunja, O Srinivasa:
here are Krishna's pastimes with the madhya beloved.

3551The madhya has manifest youth and is experienced in every way;
in mana she has three varieties: dhira and the rest.843

3552There:
[The madhya] has bashfulness and love's desire in equal measure, possesses blossoming youth,
is somewhat bold in speech, capable of union up to swooning;

3553the madhya is in mana now soft, now harsh;
in her conduct in mana she is threefold: dhira, adhira, and [combining] both.

3554The dhira-madhya, [being] in mana, here, in the precincts of this kunja,
addresses to Krishna barbed words [and] pure reproach.844

3555There:
The dhira, however, speaks to the offending beloved with barbed words, mockingly.

3556In this kunja the adhira-madhya, angry with the Lord of her life,
[speaks] fearless, cruel words that please the sakhis.

3557There:
The adhira in anger repulses the beloved with cruel words.

3558The dhira-adhira-madhya here, with tears,
speaks barbed words to Krishna, glancing at the sakhis.

3559There:
The dhira-adhira, however, speaks to the beloved with barbed words, with tears.

3560The madhya-nayika is the summit of all rasas;
the madhya Radha here bestows bliss on Krishna.

3561There:
All the excellence of rasa befits the madhya alone,
for in her innocence and boldness are plainly joined.

3562In this kunja the pragalbha, a beauty in the full bloom of youth,
displays so many artful ways to give Krishna happiness!

3563How eager she is for union cannot be told;
in her conduct in mana the pragalbha has three varieties: dhira and the rest.

3564There:
The pragalbha is in the full bloom of youth, blinded by intoxication, eager for abundant union,
versed in manifesting many bhavas, having overpowered her beloved with rasa;
her words and acts are very bold, and in mana she is extremely harsh.

3565In this kunja the dhira-pragalbha, skilled in mana,
concealing her anger, is indifferent to union.

3566There:
The dhira is indifferent in union, conceals [her feelings] and [remains] respectful.

3567The adhira-pragalbha in this nikunja house
strikes Krishna with the lotus [adorning her] ear, with cruel threats.

3568There:
The adhira, having threatened cruelly in anger, strikes the beloved.

3569The anger of the dhira-adhira-pragalbha is not noticeable;
in this kunja she threatens Krishna a little, with hints.845

3570There:
She who has the qualities of the dhira and the adhira is called dhira-adhira.

3571See, Srinivasa: in this kunja Sri Radhika,
filled with prema, moves Krishna to abhisara.

3572Sri Radhika, making abhisara in secret,
in attire suited to the time, meets Krishna.

3573The abhisarika-nayika Radhika, the beauty,
comes and meets [Him], now with the sakhis, now alone.846

3574There:
She who calls her beloved to a tryst and also goes [to him] herself —
she is the abhisarika; in attire fit for the way she [is] jyotsni or tamasi.847

3575As if hiding within her own body out of bashfulness, with all her ornaments [hushed] to silence, veiled, with one loving sakhi, let her go to her beloved.

3576The vasaka-sajja-nayika in this kunja house
joyfully, with the sakhi, prepares the bed and the rest.

3577On the path by which Krishna will come she fixes her eyes,
again and again she looks out for the messenger.

3578The vasaka-sajja-nayika Radhika, the beauty —
what actions She displays I cannot tell.

3579There:
She who, when her beloved is to come at her turn (vasaka), adorns her body
and [makes ready] the chamber — she is the vasaka-sajjika.848

3580Her actions are planning love's play, watching the path,
merry talk with the sakhi, looking again and again for the messenger, and the like.

3581In this kunja a meeting had been agreed upon;
because of Krishna's delay that eagerness faded.

3582Separation grew, the longing had no limit —
Radhika here is in the state of virahotkanthita.

3583She wonders why Krishna has not come;
[Her] actions — burning of the heart, trembling and the rest — cannot be told.

3584There:
She who longs when her blameless dearest one delays —
[her] the knowers of feelings call virahotkanthita.

3585Her actions are burning of the heart, trembling, guessing at the cause,
joylessness, shedding of tears, telling of her own state, and the like.

3586Bearing on Himself the marks of enjoyment with another beloved,
Krishna came into this kunja.

3587Glancing in great anger at the brazen nayaka,
Radha here is in the state of the khandita-nayika.

3588There:
She to whom her lover, having let the agreed time pass, having enjoyed another,
marked with the signs of enjoyment, comes [only] in the morning — she indeed is khandita.
She is given to anger, sighs, silence and the like.

3589Rai in the tamala kunja is in the state of vipralabdha:
Krishna was to come — and has not come, She ponders in Her heart.

3590This is that very tamala kunja — see, Srinivasa,
how the actions of the vipralabdha are displayed everywhere.

3591There: When, a tryst having been appointed, by fate the beloved [dear to her as] life does not come, she whose heart is tormented is called by the wise vipralabdha; [she] is given to despondency, anxious thoughts, sorrow, tears, swooning, sighs and the like.

3592Rai in this kunja is in the state of kalahantarita:
when the mana has passed, She is tormented here by remorse.

3593Her actions — incoherent speech and the rest — cannot be told;
seeing [this], the sakhis consider various means.

3594There:
She who before the sakhis in anger repulses her beloved who has come and fallen [at her feet],
and afterwards is tormented — she indeed is kalahantarita.
Her [actions] are incoherent speech, burning anguish, exhaustion, sighs and the like.849

3595Radhika here is in the state of proshita-bhartrika:
when Krishna goes to a distant land, She cannot find rest.

3596There:
When Krishna goes to a distant land, [the heroine] becomes proshita-bhartrika.850
Her [actions] are glorifying the beloved, dejection, thinness and sleeplessness,
untidiness, restlessness, numbness, anxious thoughts and the like — so it is held.

3597When Akrura, taking Krishna, was setting out for Mathura,
what Rai became here cannot be told.

3598Thus [it is said] in the poem Hamsa-duta, the second verse:
When Mukunda, the Madana of the gopis' hearts, from the house of Nanda
set out for Madhupuri, following the son of Gandini,
then Radha, suffering in separation, whirling in dense eddies, sank
into the fathomless river of anxiety whose waters are torment.851
